speaker: Hercules

text: Be on guard against men who can strike from a distance.
author: Aesop

text: Use serves to overcome dread.
author: Aesop

text: Evil wishes, like chickens, come home to roost.
author: Aesop

text: The hero is brave in deeds as well as words.
author: Aesop

text: They are not wise who give to themselves the credit due to others.
author: Aesop

text: Men often bear little grievances with less courage than they do large misfortunes.
author: Aesop

text: If men had all they wished, they would be often ruined.
author: Aesop

text: I do not care about the blows of the axe aimed at my roots, but I do grieve at being torn in pieces by these wedges made from my own branches. Misfortunes springing from ourselves are the hardest to bear.
author: Aesop
speaker: The Oak

text: A willful man will have his way to his own hurt.
author: Aesop

text: It is wise to turn circumstances to good account.
author: Aesop

text: Evil companions bring more hurt than profit.
author: Aesop

text: Forbear... harping on what was of yore, for it is the common lot of mortals to sustain the ups and downs of fortune.
author: Aesop
speaker: The Miller

text: The least outlay is not always the greatest gain.
author: Aesop

text: Children are not to be blamed for the faults of their parents.
author: Aesop

text: A Father, being on the point of death, wished to be sure that his sons would give the same attention to his farm as he himself had given it... They found no treasure, but the vines repaid their labor by an extraordinary and superabundant crop.
author: Aesop

text: We must make friends in prosperity if we would have their help in adversity.
author: Aesop

text: My sons, if you are of one mind, and unite to assist each other, you will be as this faggot, uninjured by all the attempts of your enemies; but if you are divided among yourselves, you will be broken as easily as these sticks.
author: Aesop
speaker: The Father

text: We bear all the labor, and we, not you, ought to cry out. Those who suffer most cry out the least.
author: Aesop
speaker: The Axle-Trees

text: I can't think that you, who refuse me a little matter now, will by and by confer on me a greater benefit.
author: Aesop
speaker: The Ass

text: Those who assume a character which does not belong to them, only make themselves ridiculous.
author: Aesop

text: It is easy to kick a man that is down.
author: Aesop

text: They who act without sufficient thought, will often fall into unsuspected danger.
author: Aesop

text: Benefits bestowed upon the evil-disposed increase their means of injuring you.
author: Aesop
locator: The Man Bitten by a Dog

text: The Members of the Body rebelled against the Belly... The whole Body quickly became debilitated, and the hands, feet, mouth, and eyes, when too late, repented of their folly.
author: Aesop

text: Pray help me now and scold me afterwards. Counsel without help is useless.
author: Aesop
speaker: The Boy

text: One story is good, till another is told.
author: Aesop

text: In a change of government the poor change nothing beyond the name of their master.
author: Aesop
locator: The Ass and the Old Shepherd

text: Notoriety is often mistaken for fame.
author: Aesop

text: Every man should be content to mind his own business.
author: Aesop

text: It sometimes happens that one man has all the toil, and another all the profit.
author: Aesop
locator: The Lion, the Bear, and the Fox

text: You fight and contend with the wind, and consequently you are destroyed; while we on the contrary bend before the least breath of air, and therefore remain unbroken, and escape. Stoop to conquer.
author: Aesop
speaker: The Reeds

text: It shows an evil disposition to take advantage of a friend in distress.
author: Aesop

text: Persuasion is better than Force.
author: Aesop
locator: The North Wind and the Sun

text: If you were foolish enough to sing all the summer, you must dance supperless to bed in the winter.
author: Aesop
speaker: The Ants

text: Master, how can you expect the sheep to be safe if you admit a wolf into the fold?
author: Aesop
speaker: The Dog

text: Old friends cannot with impunity be sacrificed for new ones.
author: Aesop
locator: The Goatherd and the Wild Goats

text: I should indeed be a very simple fellow if, for the chance of a greater uncertain profit, I were to forego my present certain gain.
author: Aesop
speaker: The Fisherman
locator: The Fisherman and the Little Fish

text: I do not need a trial; I know that he will be just the same as the one he chose for his companion. A man is known by the company he keeps.
author: Aesop

text: And it shall be, that every great matter they shall bring unto thee, but every small matter they shall judge: so shall it be easier for thyself, and they shall bear the burden with thee.
author: Book of Exodus
speaker: Jethro, to Moses

text: Thou wilt surely wear away, both thou, and this people that is with thee: for this thing is too heavy for thee; thou art not able to perform it thyself alone.
author: Book of Exodus
speaker: Jethro, to Moses

text: Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
author: Book of Exodus

text: Behold, the people is one, and they have all one language; and this they begin to do: and now nothing will be restrained from them, which they have imagined to do.
author: Book of Genesis
speaker: God, at Babel

text: It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.
author: Book of Genesis
speaker: God

text: Let thy mother be to thee like unto a god! Let thy father be to thee like unto a god!
author: Taittiriya Upanishad

text: Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.
author: Isaiah (Second Isaiah)

text: As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you; and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem.
author: Isaiah (Third Isaiah)

text: Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.
author: Book of Ruth
speaker: Ruth, to her mother-in-law Naomi

text: Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her.
author: Proverbs (traditionally Solomon)

text: My son, hear the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother.
author: Proverbs (traditionally Solomon)

text: Thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine by the sides of thine house: thy children like olive plants round about thy table.
author: Psalms

text: Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him.
author: Psalms (traditionally David)

text: God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains.
author: Psalms (traditionally David)

text: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
author: Psalms (traditionally David)

text: Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.
author: Psalms (traditionally Solomon)

text: The quality of decision is like the well-timed swoop of a falcon which enables it to strike and destroy its victim.... Therefore the good fighter will be terrible in his onset, and prompt in his decision.
author: Sun Tzu

text: The art of war is of vital importance to the State.... It is a matter of life and death, a road either to safety or to ruin. Hence it is a subject of inquiry which can on no account be neglected.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Be stern in the council-chamber,... so that you may control the situation.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 64

text: If a general shows confidence in his men but always insists on his orders being obeyed,... the gain will be mutual.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter IX, The Army on the March, verse 45

text: Now a soldier's spirit is keenest in the morning;... by noonday it has begun to flag; and in the evening, his mind is bent only on returning to camp.
author: Sun Tzu

text: You may advance and be absolutely irresistible, if you make for the enemy's weak points; you may retire and be safe from pursuit if your movements are more rapid than those of the enemy.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 10

text: Hold out baits to entice the enemy. Feign disorder, and crush him.... If he is secure at all points, be prepared for him. If he is in superior strength, evade him.
author: Sun Tzu

text: What enables the wise sovereign and the good general to strike and conquer, and achieve things beyond the reach of ordinary men, is foreknowledge.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XIII, The Use of Spies, verse 4

text: To begin by bluster, but afterwards to take fright at the enemy's numbers, shows a supreme lack of intelligence.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter IX, The Army on the March, verse 37

text: To secure ourselves against defeat lies in our own hands, but the opportunity of defeating the enemy is provided by the enemy himself.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Without constant practice, the officers will be nervous and undecided when mustering for battle; without constant practice, the general will be wavering and irresolute when the crisis is at hand.
author: Sun Tzu
speaker: Wang Tzu, quoted by Tu Yu

text: Though an obstinate fight may be made by a small force, in the end it must be captured by the larger force.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter III, Attack by Stratagem, verse 10

text: The general, unable to control his irritation, will launch his men to the assault like swarming ants,... with the result that one-third of his men are slain, while the town still remains untaken.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter III, Attack by Stratagem, verse 5

text: He who exercises no forethought but makes light of his opponents is sure to be captured by them.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter IX, The Army on the March, verse 41

text: To see victory only when it is within the ken of the common herd is not the acme of excellence.
author: Sun Tzu

text: If you are careful of your men,... and camp on hard ground, the army will be free from disease of every kind.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter IX, The Army on the March, verse 12

text: Knowing the place and the time of the coming battle, we may concentrate from the greatest distances in order to fight.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 19

text: The clever combatant imposes his will on the enemy, but does not allow the enemy's will to be imposed on him.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 2

text: The general who is skilled in defence hides in the most secret recesses of the earth;... he who is skilled in attack flashes forth from the topmost heights of heaven.
author: Sun Tzu

text: What the ancients called a clever fighter is one who not only wins, but excels in winning with ease.... Hence his victories bring him neither reputation for wisdom nor credit for courage.
author: Sun Tzu

text: That the impact of your army may be like a grindstone dashed against an egg, this is effected by the science of weak points and strong.
author: Sun Tzu

text: The warlike prince controls his soldiers by his authority, kits them together by good faith, and by rewards makes them serviceable.
author: Sun Tzu
speaker: Tu Mu, quoting the San Lueh
locator: Chapter XII, The Attack by Fire, verse 16, commentary

text: Simulated disorder postulates perfect discipline; simulated fear postulates courage; simulated weakness postulates strength.
author: Sun Tzu

text: The only chance of life lies in giving up all hope of it.
author: Sun Tzu
speaker: Mei Yao-ch'en
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 50

text: Place your army in deadly peril, and it will survive; plunge it into desperate straits, and it will come off in safety.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 58

text: It is precisely when a force has fallen into harm's way that is capable of striking a blow for victory.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 59

text: Now the general is the bulwark of the State: if the bulwark is complete at all points; the State will be strong; if the bulwark is defective, the State will be weak.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter III, Attack by Stratagem, verse 11

text: He will win who, prepared himself, waits to take the enemy unprepared.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter III, Attack by Stratagem, verse 17

text: All men can see the tactics whereby I conquer, but what none can see is the strategy out of which victory is evolved.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 27

text: The captured soldiers should be kindly treated and kept.... This is called, using the conquered foe to augment one's own strength.
author: Sun Tzu

text: At the critical moment, the leader of an army acts like one who has climbed up a height and then kicks away the ladder behind him.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 38

text: To lift an autumn hair is no sign of great strength;... to see sun and moon is no sign of sharp sight; to hear the noise of thunder is no sign of a quick ear.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Disciplined and calm, to await the appearance of disorder and hubbub amongst the enemy: this is the art of retaining self-possession.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Fighting with a large army under your command is nowise different from fighting with a small one: it is merely a question of instituting signs and signals.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Do not repeat the tactics which have gained you one victory, but let your methods be regulated by the infinite variety of circumstances.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 28

text: If you set a fully equipped army in march in order to snatch an advantage, the chances are that you will be too late. On the other hand, to detach a flying column for the purpose involves the sacrifice of its baggage and stores.
author: Sun Tzu

text: We can form a single united body, while the enemy must split up into fractions. Hence there will be a whole pitted against separate parts of a whole, which means that we shall be many to the enemy's few.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 14

text: The end and aim of spying in all its five varieties is knowledge of the enemy; and this knowledge can only be derived, in the first instance, from the converted spy.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XIII, The Use of Spies, verse 25

text: By holding out advantages to him, he can cause the enemy to approach of his own accord; or, by inflicting damage, he can make it impossible for the enemy to draw near.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 3

text: With his forces intact he will dispute the mastery of the Empire, and thus, without losing a man, his triumph will be complete.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter III, Attack by Stratagem, verse 7

text: Soldiers when in desperate straits lose the sense of fear. If there is no place of refuge, they will stand firm. If they are in the heart of a hostile country, they will show a stubborn front. If there is no help for it, they will fight hard.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 24

text: For should the enemy strengthen his van, he will weaken his rear; should he strengthen his rear, he will weaken his van; should he strengthen his left, he will weaken his right; should he strengthen his right, he will weaken his left. If he sends reinforcements everywhere, he will everywhere be weak.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 17

text: On dispersive ground, I would inspire my men with unity of purpose.... On facile ground, I would see that there is close connection between all parts of my army.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 46

text: You can be sure of succeeding in your attacks if you only attack places which are undefended.... You can ensure the safety of your defence if you only hold positions that cannot be attacked.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 7

text: Numerical weakness comes from having to prepare against possible attacks; numerical strength, from compelling our adversary to make these preparations against us.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 18

text: Appear at points which the enemy must hasten to defend; march swiftly to places where you are not expected.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 5

text: In war, then, let your great object be victory, not lengthy campaigns.
author: Sun Tzu

text: He will win who knows how to handle both superior and inferior forces.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter III, Attack by Stratagem, verse 17

text: We may take it then that an army without its baggage-train is lost; without provisions it is lost; without bases of supply it is lost.
author: Sun Tzu

text: O divine art of subtlety and secrecy! Through you we learn to be invisible, through you inaudible;... and hence we can hold the enemy's fate in our hands.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 9

text: Even though the enemy should offer us an attractive bait,... it will be advisable not to stir forth, but rather to retreat, thus enticing the enemy in his turn.
author: Sun Tzu

text: If there is disturbance in the camp, the general's authority is weak. If the banners and flags are shifted about, sedition is afoot. If the officers are angry, it means that the men are weary.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter IX, The Army on the March, verse 33

text: A wise general makes a point of foraging on the enemy. One cartload of the enemy's provisions is equivalent to twenty of one's own.
author: Sun Tzu

text: If soldiers are punished before they have grown attached to you, they will not prove submissive; and, unless submissive, then will be practically useless. If, when the soldiers have become attached to you, punishments are not enforced, they will still be useless.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter IX, The Army on the March, verse 42

text: By commanding the army to advance or to retreat, being ignorant of the fact that it cannot obey. This is called hobbling the army.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter III, Attack by Stratagem, verse 13

text: Spies cannot be usefully employed without a certain intuitive sagacity.... They cannot be properly managed without benevolence and straightforwardness.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XIII, The Use of Spies, verse 15-16

text: If fighting is sure to result in victory, then you must fight, even though the ruler forbid it; if fighting will not result in victory, then you must not fight even at the ruler's bidding.
author: Sun Tzu

text: If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles. If you know yourself but not the enemy, for every victory gained you will also suffer a defeat.... If you know neither the enemy nor yourself, you will succumb in every battle.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter III, Attack by Stratagem, verse 18

text: It is the business of a general to be quiet and thus ensure secrecy; upright and just, and thus maintain order.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 35

text: In all fighting, the direct method may be used for joining battle, but indirect methods will be needed in order to secure victory.
author: Sun Tzu

text: When you surround an army, leave an outlet free.... Do not press a desperate foe too hard.
author: Sun Tzu

text: We cannot enter into alliance with neighbouring princes until we are acquainted with their designs.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 52

text: The clever combatant looks to the effect of combined energy, and does not require too much from individuals.... Hence his ability to pick out the right men and utilise combined energy.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Carefully compare the opposing army with your own, so that you may know where strength is superabundant and where it is deficient.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 24

text: If your opponent is of choleric temper, seek to irritate him. Pretend to be weak, that he may grow arrogant.
author: Sun Tzu

text: If he is taking his ease, give him no rest.... If his forces are united, separate them.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Energy may be likened to the bending of a crossbow; decision, to the releasing of the trigger.
author: Sun Tzu

text: When the common soldiers are too strong and their officers too weak, the result is insubordination.... When the officers are too strong and the common soldiers too weak, the result is collapse.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Without harmony in the State, no military expedition can be undertaken; without harmony in the army, no battle array can be formed.
author: Sun Tzu
speaker: Wu Tzu, quoted by Chang Yu

text: When an army is overthrown and its leader slain, the cause will surely be found among these five dangerous faults. Let them be a subject of meditation.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VIII, Variation of Tactics, verse 14

text: The seeker after glory should be careless of public opinion.
author: Sun Tzu
speaker: Mei Yao-ch'en
locator: Chapter VIII, Variation of Tactics, verse 12

text: In hemmed-in situations, you must resort to stratagem. In a desperate position, you must fight.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VIII, Variation of Tactics, verse 2

text: The further you penetrate into a country, the greater will be the solidarity of your troops, and thus the defenders will not prevail against you.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 20

text: The principle on which to manage an army is to set up one standard of courage which all must reach.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 32

text: The skilful fighter puts himself into a position which makes defeat impossible, and does not miss the moment for defeating the enemy.
author: Sun Tzu

text: The skilful general conducts his army just as though he were leading a single man, willy-nilly, by the hand.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 34

text: He who knows these things, and in fighting puts his knowledge into practice, will win his battles. He who knows them not, nor practises them, will surely be defeated.
author: Sun Tzu

text: We shall be unable to turn natural advantages to account unless we make use of local guides.
author: Sun Tzu

text: If you know the enemy and know yourself, your victory will not stand in doubt; if you know Heaven and know Earth, you may make your victory complete.
author: Sun Tzu

text: When he keeps aloof and tries to provoke a battle, he is anxious for the other side to advance.... If his place of encampment is easy of access, he is tendering a bait.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter IX, The Army on the March, verse 19-20

text: If the enemy sees an advantage to be gained and makes no effort to secure it, the soldiers are exhausted.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter IX, The Army on the March, verse 31

text: The good fighters of old first put themselves beyond the possibility of defeat, and then waited for an opportunity of defeating the enemy.
author: Sun Tzu

text: The Commander stands for the virtues of wisdom, sincerity, benevolence, courage and strictness.
author: Sun Tzu

text: The enlightened ruler lays his plans well ahead; the good general cultivates his resources.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XII, The Attack by Fire, verse 16

text: One who is skilful at keeping the enemy on the move maintains deceitful appearances, according to which the enemy will act.... He sacrifices something, that the enemy may snatch at it.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Throw your soldiers into positions whence there is no escape, and they will prefer death to flight. If they will face death, there is nothing they may not achieve.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 23

text: Hostile armies may face each other for years, striving for the victory which is decided in a single day.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XIII, The Use of Spies, verse 2

text: The Moral Law causes the people to be in complete accord with their ruler, so that they will follow him regardless of their lives, undismayed by any danger.
author: Sun Tzu

text: The general who advances without coveting fame and retreats without fearing disgrace,... whose only thought is to protect his country and do good service for his sovereign, is the jewel of the kingdom.
author: Sun Tzu

text: To fight and conquer in all your battles is not supreme excellence; supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy's resistance without fighting.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter III, Attack by Stratagem, verse 2

text: We cannot enter into alliances until we are acquainted with the designs of our neighbours.
author: Sun Tzu

text: The direct and the indirect lead on to each other in turn. It is like moving in a circle, you never come to an end. Who can exhaust the possibilities of their combination?
author: Sun Tzu

text: Now, when your weapons are dulled, your ardour damped, your strength exhausted and your treasure spent, other chieftains will spring up to take advantage of your extremity. Then no man, however wise, will be able to avert the consequences that must ensue.
author: Sun Tzu

text: If we wish to fight, the enemy can be forced to an engagement even though he be sheltered behind a high rampart and a deep ditch. All we need do is attack some other place that he will be obliged to relieve.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 11

text: For the men of Wu and the men of Yüeh are enemies;... yet if they are crossing a river in the same boat and are caught by a storm, they will come to each other's assistance just as the left hand helps the right.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 30

text: The consummate leader cultivates the moral law, and strictly adheres to method and discipline; thus it is in his power to control success.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Though we have heard of stupid haste in war, cleverness has never been seen associated with long delays.... There is no instance of a country having benefited from prolonged warfare.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Attack him where he is unprepared, appear where you are not expected.... These military devices, leading to victory, must not be divulged beforehand.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Do not pursue an enemy who simulates flight; do not attack soldiers whose temper is keen.... Do not swallow a bait offered by the enemy.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Keep your army continually on the move,... and devise unfathomable plans.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 22

text: No ruler should put troops into the field merely to gratify his own spleen; no general should fight a battle simply out of pique.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XII, The Attack by Fire, verse 18

text: By altering his arrangements and changing his plans,... he keeps the enemy without definite knowledge.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 37

text: It is that in war the victorious strategist only seeks battle after the victory has been won, whereas he who is destined to defeat first fights and afterwards looks for victory.
author: Sun Tzu

text: When a warlike prince attacks a powerful state, his generalship shows itself in preventing the concentration of the enemy's forces. He overawes his opponents, and their allies are prevented from joining against him.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 54

text: Whether to concentrate or to divide your troops, must be decided by circumstances.
author: Sun Tzu

text: If the enemy is unprepared, you may sally forth and defeat him. But if the enemy is prepared for your coming, and you fail to defeat him, then, return being impossible, disaster will ensue.
author: Sun Tzu

text: If it is to your advantage, make a forward move; if not, stay where you are.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XII, The Attack by Fire, verse 19

text: He wins his battles by making no mistakes.... Making no mistakes is what establishes the certainty of victory, for it means conquering an enemy that is already defeated.
author: Sun Tzu

text: It is only the enlightened ruler and the wise general who will use the highest intelligence of the army for purposes of spying and thereby they achieve great results.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XIII, The Use of Spies, verse 27

text: When a general, unable to estimate the enemy's strength, allows an inferior force to engage a larger one, or hurls a weak detachment against a powerful one, and neglects to place picked soldiers in the front rank, the result must be a rout.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Without waiting to be asked, they will do your will;... without restrictions, they will be faithful; without giving orders, they can be trusted.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 25

text: The host thus forming a single united body, is it impossible either for the brave to advance alone, or for the cowardly to retreat alone.... This is the art of handling large masses of men.
author: Sun Tzu

text: The good fighter is able to secure himself against defeat,... but cannot make certain of defeating the enemy.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Begin by seizing something which your opponent holds dear; then he will be amenable to your will.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 18

text: The spot where we intend to fight must not be made known; for then the enemy will have to prepare against a possible attack at several different points.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 16

text: Forestall your opponent by seizing what he holds dear,... and subtly contrive to time his arrival on the ground.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 66

text: It may be known that the leader of armies is the arbiter of the people's fate, the man on whom it depends whether the nation shall be in peace or in peril.
author: Sun Tzu

text: By discovering the enemy's dispositions and remaining invisible ourselves, we can keep our forces concentrated, while the enemy's must be divided.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 13

text: The general who does not understand these, may be well acquainted with the configuration of the country, yet he will not be able to turn his knowledge to practical account.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VIII, Variation of Tactics, verse 5

text: Military tactics are like unto water; for water in its natural course runs away from high places and hastens downwards.... So in war, the way is to avoid what is strong and to strike at what is weak.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 29-30

text: If the enemy leaves a door open, you must rush in.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 65

text: The natural formation of the country is the soldier's best ally;... but a power of estimating the adversary, of controlling the forces of victory, and of shrewdly calculating difficulties, dangers and distances, constitutes the test of a great general.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Move not unless you see an advantage; use not your troops unless there is something to be gained; fight not unless the position is critical.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XII, The Attack by Fire, verse 17

text: Manoeuvering with an army is advantageous; with an undisciplined multitude, most dangerous.
author: Sun Tzu

text: In making tactical dispositions, the highest pitch you can attain is to conceal them;... conceal your dispositions, and you will be safe from the prying of the subtlest spies, from the machinations of the wisest brains.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 25

text: The art of war teaches us to rely not on the likelihood of the enemy's not coming, but on our own readiness to receive him; not on the chance of his not attacking, but rather on the fact that we have made our position unassailable.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VIII, Variation of Tactics, verse 11

text: When he utilises combined energy, his fighting men become as it were like unto rolling logs or stones.
author: Sun Tzu

text: To be near the goal while the enemy is still far from it, to wait at ease while the enemy is toiling and struggling, to be well-fed while the enemy is famished: this is the art of husbanding one's strength.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Regard your soldiers as your children, and they will follow you into the deepest valleys; look on them as your own beloved sons, and they will stand by you even unto death.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Confront your soldiers with the deed itself; never let them know your design.... When the outlook is bright, bring it before their eyes; but tell them nothing when the situation is gloomy.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 57

text: Without subtle ingenuity of mind, one cannot make certain of the truth of their reports.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XIII, The Use of Spies, verse 17

text: Security against defeat implies defensive tactics; ability to defeat the enemy means taking the offensive.... Standing on the defensive indicates insufficient strength; attacking, a superabundance of strength.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Just as water retains no constant shape, so in warfare there are no constant conditions.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 32

text: Now the general who wins a battle makes many calculations in his temple ere the battle is fought.
author: Sun Tzu

text: The difficulty of tactical manoeuvering consists in turning the devious into the direct, and misfortune into gain.
author: Sun Tzu

text: It is that with none in the whole army are more intimate relations to be maintained than with spies.... None should be more liberally rewarded. In no other business should greater secrecy be preserved.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XIII, The Use of Spies, verse 14

text: If neither time nor place be known, then the left wing will be impotent to succour the right, the right equally impotent to succour the left, the van unable to relieve the rear, or the rear to support the van.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 20

text: The general who loses a battle makes but few calculations beforehand. Thus do many calculations lead to victory, and few calculations to defeat: how much more no calculation at all!
author: Sun Tzu

text: If, on the other hand, in the midst of difficulties we are always ready to seize an advantage, we may extricate ourselves from misfortune.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VIII, Variation of Tactics, verse 9

text: Humble words and increased preparations are signs that the enemy is about to advance.... Violent language and driving forward as if to the attack are signs that he will retreat.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter IX, The Army on the March, verse 24

text: Water shapes its course according to the nature of the ground over which it flows; the soldier works out his victory in relation to the foe whom he is facing.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 31

text: When you engage in actual fighting, if victory is long in coming, the men's weapons will grow dull and their ardour will be damped. If you lay siege to a town, you will exhaust your strength.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Over-solicitude for his men, which exposes him to worry and trouble.... These are the five besetting sins of a general, ruinous to the conduct of war.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VIII, Variation of Tactics, verse 12-13

text: The enlightened ruler is heedful, and the good general full of caution. This is the way to keep a country at peace and an army intact.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XII, The Attack by Fire, verse 22

text: When the higher officers are angry and insubordinate, and on meeting the enemy give battle on their own account from a feeling of resentment, before the commander-in-chief can tell whether or no he is in a position to fight, the result is ruin.
author: Sun Tzu

text: The experienced soldier, once in motion, is never bewildered; once he has broken camp, he is never at a loss.
author: Sun Tzu

text: A victorious army opposed to a routed one, is as a pound's weight placed in the scale against a single grain.
author: Sun Tzu

text: To remain in ignorance of the enemy's condition simply because one grudges the outlay of a hundred ounces of silver in honours and emoluments,... is the height of inhumanity.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XIII, The Use of Spies, verse 2-3

text: Unhappy is the fate of one who tries to win his battles and succeed in his attacks without cultivating the spirit of enterprise; for the result is waste of time and general stagnation.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XII, The Attack by Fire, verse 15

text: If we do not wish to fight, we can prevent the enemy from engaging us even though the lines of our encampment be merely traced out on the ground. All we need do is to throw something odd and unaccountable in his way.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 12

text: When the army is restless and distrustful, trouble is sure to come from the other feudal princes. This is simply bringing anarchy into the army, and flinging victory away.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter III, Attack by Stratagem, verse 16

text: It is only one who is thoroughly acquainted with the evils of war that can thoroughly understand the profitable way of carrying it on.
author: Sun Tzu

text: The general who thoroughly understands the advantages that accompany variation of tactics knows how to handle his troops.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VIII, Variation of Tactics, verse 4

text: If in training soldiers commands are habitually enforced, the army will be well-disciplined; if not, its discipline will be bad.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter IX, The Army on the March, verse 44

text: Raising a host of a hundred thousand men and marching them great distances entails heavy loss on the people and a drain on the resources of the State.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XIII, The Use of Spies, verse 1

text: If they are in an awkward place together, they will surely exert their united strength to get out of it.
author: Sun Tzu
speaker: Chang Yu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, commentary

text: Regard your soldiers as your children, and they will follow you into the deepest valleys; look upon them as your own beloved sons, and they will stand by you even unto death.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Ponder and deliberate before you make a move.
author: Sun Tzu

text: He will win whose army is animated by the same spirit throughout all its ranks.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter III, Attack by Stratagem, verse 17

text: The sight of men whispering together in small knots or speaking in subdued tones points to disaffection amongst the rank and file.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter IX, The Army on the March, verse 35

text: Whoever is first in the field and awaits the coming of the enemy, will be fresh for the fight; whoever is second in the field and has to hasten to battle, will arrive exhausted.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 1

text: If we know that our own men are in a condition to attack, but are unaware that the enemy is not open to attack, we have gone only halfway towards victory.
author: Sun Tzu

text: To refrain from intercepting an enemy whose banners are in perfect order, to refrain from attacking an army drawn up in calm and confident array: this is the art of studying circumstances.
author: Sun Tzu

text: The skilful leader subdues the enemy's troops without any fighting; he captures their cities without laying siege to them; he overthrows their kingdom without lengthy operations in the field.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter III, Attack by Stratagem, verse 6

text: The energy developed by good fighting men is as the momentum of a round stone rolled down a mountain thousands of feet in height.
author: Sun Tzu

text: When envoys are sent with compliments in their mouths, it is a sign that the enemy wishes for a truce.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter IX, The Army on the March, verse 38

text: He who can modify his tactics in relation to his opponent and thereby succeed in winning, may be called a heaven-born captain.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 33

text: All warfare is based on deception.... Hence, when able to attack, we must seem unable; when using our forces, we must seem inactive; when we are near, we must make the enemy believe we are far away; when far away, we must make him believe we are near.
author: Sun Tzu

text: When these five kinds of spy are all at work, none can discover the secret system. This is called "divine manipulation of the threads." It is the sovereign's most precious faculty.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XIII, The Use of Spies, verse 8

text: Let your plans be dark and impenetrable as night, and when you move, fall like a thunderbolt.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Success in warfare is gained by carefully accommodating ourselves to the enemy's purpose.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 60

text: We may know that there are five essentials for victory: (1) He will win who knows when to fight and when not to fight.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter III, Attack by Stratagem, verse 17

text: When invading hostile territory, the general principle is, that penetrating deeply brings cohesion; penetrating but a short way means dispersion.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 42

text: In the practical art of war, the best thing of all is to take the enemy's country whole and intact; to shatter and destroy it is not so good.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter III, Attack by Stratagem, verse 1

text: Now an army is exposed to six several calamities, not arising from natural causes, but from faults for which the general is responsible.
author: Sun Tzu

text: A clever general, therefore, avoids an army when its spirit is keen, but attacks it when it is sluggish and inclined to return. This is the art of studying moods.
author: Sun Tzu

text: The highest form of generalship is to baulk the enemy's plans;... and the worst policy of all is to besiege walled cities.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter III, Attack by Stratagem, verse 3

text: In the wise leader's plans, considerations of advantage and of disadvantage will be blended together.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VIII, Variation of Tactics, verse 7

text: If, however, you are indulgent, but unable to make your authority felt; kind-hearted, but unable to enforce your commands; and incapable, moreover, of quelling disorder: then your soldiers must be likened to spoilt children; they are useless for any practical purpose.
author: Sun Tzu

text: You will at once act for the benefit of your soldiers and utilise the natural advantages of the ground.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter IX, The Army on the March, verse 13

text: According as circumstances are favourable, one should modify one's plans.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Soldiers must be treated in the first instance with humanity, but kept under control by means of iron discipline.... This is a certain road to victory.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter IX, The Army on the March, verse 43

text: Carefully study the well-being of your men,... and do not overtax them. Concentrate your energy and hoard your strength.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 22

text: In war, practise dissimulation, and you will succeed.... Move only if there is a real advantage to be gained.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Gongs and drums, banners and flags, are means whereby the ears and eyes of the host may be focussed on one particular point.
author: Sun Tzu

text: A general ought in time of peace to show kindly confidence in his men and also make his authority respected, so that when they come to face the enemy, orders may be executed and discipline maintained, because they all trust and look up to him.
author: Sun Tzu
speaker: Tu Mu
locator: Chapter IX, The Army on the March, verse 45, commentary

text: There are not more than five musical notes, yet the combinations of these five give rise to more melodies than can ever be heard.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Rapidity is the essence of war:... take advantage of the enemy's unreadiness, make your way by unexpected routes, and attack unguarded spots.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter XI, The Nine Situations, verse 19

text: In battle, there are not more than two methods of attack, the direct and the indirect; yet these two in combination give rise to an endless series of manoeuvers.
author: Sun Tzu

text: Peace proposals unaccompanied by a sworn covenant indicate a plot.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter IX, The Army on the March, verse 26

text: There are roads which must not be followed,... positions which must not be contested, commands of the sovereign which must not be obeyed.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VIII, Variation of Tactics, verse 3

text: That general is skilful in attack whose opponent does not know what to defend; and he is skilful in defence whose opponent does not know what to attack.
author: Sun Tzu
locator: Chapter VI, Weak Points and Strong, verse 8

text: So long, Ananda, as the Vaggians meet together in concord, and rise in concord, and carry out their undertakings in concord, so long may the Vaggians be expected not to decline, but to prosper.
author: Gautama Buddha

text: The mean man is difficult to serve, and easy to please. If you try to please him, though it be in a way which is not accordant with right, he may be pleased. But in his employment of men, he wishes them to be equal to everything.
author: Confucius

text: A prince should employ his minister according to according to the rules of propriety; ministers should serve their prince with faithfulness.
author: Confucius

text: The reason why the ancients did not readily give utterance to their words, was that they feared lest their actions should not come up to them.
author: Confucius

text: The superior man bends his attention to what is radical. That being established, all practical courses naturally grow up. Filial piety and fraternal submission! Are they not the root of all benevolent actions?
author: Confucius
speaker: Youzi (the philosopher Yu)

text: I am not concerned that I have no place, I am concerned how I may fit myself for one. I am not concerned that I am not known, I seek to be worthy to be known.
author: Confucius

text: Though a man have abilities as admirable as those of the Duke of Chau, yet if he be proud and niggardly, those other things are really not worth being looked at.
author: Confucius

text: There are three errors to which they who stand in the presence of a man of virtue and station are liable. They may speak when it does not come to them to speak; this is called rashness. They may not speak when it comes to them to speak; this is called concealment. They may speak without looking at the countenance of their superior; this is called blindness.
author: Confucius

text: Shih goes beyond the due mean, and Shang does not come up to it... To go beyond is as wrong as to fall short.
author: Confucius

text: Suppose that there is an individual who can be entrusted with the charge of a young orphan prince, and can be commissioned with authority over a state of a hundred li, and whom no emergency however great can drive from his principles: is such a man a superior man? He is a superior man indeed.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zengzi (the philosopher Tsang)

text: Is virtue a thing remote? I wish to be virtuous, and lo! virtue is at hand.
author: Confucius

text: The superior man holds righteousness to be of highest importance. A man in a superior situation, having valour without righteousness, will be guilty of insubordination; one of the lower people having valour without righteousness, will commit robbery.
author: Confucius

text: The superior man does not promote a man simply on account of his words, nor does he put aside good words because of the man.
author: Confucius

text: If names be not correct, language is not in accordance with the truth of things. If language be not in accordance with the truth of things, affairs cannot be carried on to success.
author: Confucius

text: Good government obtains, when those who are near are made happy, and those who are far off are attracted.
author: Confucius

text: I do not know how a man without truthfulness is to get on. How can a large carriage be made to go without the cross-bar for yoking the oxen to, or a small carriage without the arrangement for yoking the horses?
author: Confucius

text: The superior man, having obtained their confidence, may then impose labours on his people. If he have not gained their confidence, they will think that he is oppressing them. Having obtained the confidence of his prince, one may then remonstrate with him. If he have not gained his confidence, the prince will think that he is vilifying him.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zixia (Tsze-hsia)

text: The superior man on grounds of culture meets with his friends, and by their friendship helps his virtue.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zengzi (the philosopher Tsang)

text: The superior man wishes to be slow in his speech and earnest in his conduct.
author: Confucius

text: In festive ceremonies, it is better to be sparing than extravagant. In the ceremonies of mourning, it is better that there be deep sorrow than a minute attention to observances.
author: Confucius

text: Is any one able for one day to apply his strength to virtue? I have not seen the case in which his strength would be insufficient.
author: Confucius

text: He with whom neither slander that gradually soaks into the mind, nor statements that startle like a wound in the flesh, are successful, may be called intelligent indeed.
author: Confucius

text: When the year becomes cold, then we know how the pine and the cypress are the last to lose their leaves.
author: Confucius

text: Things that are done, it is needless to speak about; things that have had their course, it is needless to remonstrate about; things that are past, it is needless to blame.
author: Confucius

text: The doctrine of our master is to be true to the principles of our nature and the benevolent exercise of them to others, this and nothing more.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zengzi (the philosopher Tsang)

text: Specious words confound virtue. Want of forbearance in small matters confounds great plans.
author: Confucius

text: When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it; this is knowledge.
author: Confucius

text: The art of governing is to keep its affairs before the mind without weariness, and to practise them with undeviating consistency.
author: Confucius

text: To put the people to death without having instructed them; this is called cruelty. To require from them, suddenly, the full tale of work, without having given them warning; this is called oppression.
author: Confucius

text: When a man's knowledge is sufficient to attain, and his virtue is not sufficient to enable him to hold, whatever he may have gained, he will lose again.
author: Confucius

text: The man who is fond of daring and is dissatisfied with poverty, will proceed to insubordination. So will the man who is not virtuous, when you carry your dislike of him to an extreme.
author: Confucius

text: How can he be used as a guide to a blind man, who does not support him when tottering, nor raise him up when fallen?
author: Confucius
speaker: Confucius, quoting Chau Zan

text: When we see men of worth, we should think of equalling them; when we see men of a contrary character, we should turn inwards and examine ourselves.
author: Confucius

text: I do not open up the truth to one who is not eager to get knowledge, nor help out any one who is not anxious to explain himself. When I have presented one corner of a subject to any one, and he cannot from it learn the other three, I do not repeat my lesson.
author: Confucius

text: The superior man seeks to perfect the admirable qualities of men, and does not seek to perfect their bad qualities. The mean man does the opposite of this.
author: Confucius

text: Extravagance leads to insubordination, and parsimony to meanness. It is better to be mean than to be insubordinate.
author: Confucius

text: There are learning extensively, and having a firm and sincere aim; inquiring with earnestness, and reflecting with self-application: virtue is in such a course.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zixia (Tsze-hsia)

text: While a man's father is alive, look at the bent of his will; when his father is dead, look at his conduct. If for three years he does not alter from the way of his father, he may be called filial.
author: Confucius

text: When a country is well-governed, poverty and a mean condition are things to be ashamed of. When a country is ill- governed, riches and honour are things to be ashamed of.
author: Confucius

text: If a minister make his own conduct correct, what difficulty will he have in assisting in government? If he cannot rectify himself, what has he to do with rectifying others?
author: Confucius

text: Contemplating good, and pursuing it, as if they could not reach it; contemplating evil, and shrinking from it, as they would from thrusting the hand into boiling water: I have seen such men, as I have heard such words.
author: Confucius

text: The stable being burned down, when he was at court, on his return he said, 'Has any man been hurt?' He did not ask about the horses.
author: Confucius

text: It is only the (truly) virtuous man, who can love, or who can hate, others.
author: Confucius

text: Hear much and put aside the points of which you stand in doubt, while you speak cautiously at the same time of the others: then you will afford few occasions for blame. See much and put aside the things which seem perilous, while you are cautious at the same time in carrying the others into practice: then you will have few occasions for repentance.
author: Confucius

text: He is earnest in what he is doing, and careful in his speech; he frequents the company of men of principle that he may be rectified: such a person may be said indeed to love to learn.
author: Confucius

text: Let every man consider virtue as what devolves on himself. He may not yield the performance of it even to his teacher.
author: Confucius

text: The superior man may indeed have to endure want, but the mean man, when he is in want, gives way to unbridled license.
author: Confucius

text: We should be apprehensive and cautious, as if on the brink of a deep gulf, as if treading on thin ice.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zengzi (the philosopher Tsang), quoting the Book of Poetry

text: The superior man is modest in his speech, but exceeds in his actions.
author: Confucius

text: A superior man may be made to go to the well, but he cannot be made to go down into it. He may be imposed upon, but he cannot be fooled.
author: Confucius

text: Faithfully admonish your friend, and skillfully lead him on. If you find him impracticable, stop. Do not disgrace yourself.
author: Confucius

text: A youth is to be regarded with respect. How do we know that his future will not be equal to our present?
author: Confucius

text: To be poor without murmuring is difficult. To be rich without being proud is easy.
author: Confucius

text: Can there be love which does not lead to strictness with its object? Can there be loyalty which does not lead to the instruction of its object?
author: Confucius

text: There are three principles of conduct which the man of high rank should consider specially important: that in his deportment and manner he keep from violence and heedlessness; that in regulating his countenance he keep near to sincerity; and that in his words and tones he keep far from lowness and impropriety.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zengzi (the philosopher Tsang)

text: When any of his friends died, if he had no relations who could be depended on for the necessary offices, he would say, 'I will bury him.'
author: Confucius

text: If, in my person, I commit offences, they are not to be attributed to you, the people of the myriad regions. If you in the myriad regions commit offences, these offences must rest on my person.
author: Confucius
speaker: King T'ang

text: Go before the people with your example, and be laborious in their affairs... Be not weary (in these things).
author: Confucius

text: The rulers have failed in their duties, and the people consequently have been disorganised, for a long time. When you have found out the truth of any accusation, be grieved for and pity them, and do not feel joy at your own ability.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zengzi (the philosopher Tsang)

text: He who offends against Heaven has none to whom he can pray.
author: Confucius

text: May not Shun be instanced as having governed efficiently without exertion? What did he do? He did nothing but gravely and reverently occupy his royal seat.
author: Confucius

text: In my dealings with men, whose evil do I blame, whose goodness do I praise, beyond what is proper? If I do sometimes exceed in praise, there must be ground for it in my examination of the individual.
author: Confucius

text: Is there one word which may serve as a rule of practice for all one's life?' The Master said, 'Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
author: Confucius

text: The scholar, trained for public duty, seeing threatening danger, is prepared to sacrifice his life. When the opportunity of gain is presented to him, he thinks of righteousness.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zizhang (Tsze-chang)

text: Serving men in an upright way, where shall I go to, and not experience such a thrice- repeated dismissal? If I choose to serve men in a crooked way, what necessity is there for me to leave the country of my parents?
author: Confucius
speaker: Hui of Liu-hsia

text: When I walk along with two others, they may serve me as my teachers. I will select their good qualities and follow them, their bad qualities and avoid them.
author: Confucius

text: What the superior man seeks, is in himself. What the mean man seeks, is in others.
author: Confucius

text: They who know the truth are not equal to those who love it, and they who love it are not equal to those who delight in it.
author: Confucius

text: Generally, in the giving pay or rewards to men, to do it in a stingy way; this is called acting the part of a mere official.
author: Confucius

text: The things in reference to which the Master exercised the greatest caution were, fasting, war, and sickness.
author: Confucius

text: The superior man undergoes three changes. Looked at from a distance, he appears stern; when approached, he is mild; when he is heard to speak, his language is firm and decided.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zixia (Tsze-hsia)

text: Let the superior man never fail reverentially to order his own conduct, and let him be respectful to others and observant of propriety: then all within the four seas will be his brothers. What has the superior man to do with being distressed because he has no brothers?
author: Confucius
speaker: Zixia (Tsze-hsia)

text: For one word a man is often deemed to be wise, and for one word he is often deemed to be foolish. We ought to be careful indeed in what we say.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zigong (Tsze-kung)

text: When a number of people are together, for a whole day, without their conversation turning on righteousness, and when they are fond of carrying out the suggestions of a small shrewdness; theirs is indeed a hard case.
author: Confucius

text: The man of virtue makes the difficulty to be overcome his first business, and success only a subsequent consideration; this may be called perfect virtue.
author: Confucius

text: The days and months are passing away; the years do not wait for us.
author: Confucius
speaker: Yang Ho

text: The mind of the superior man is conversant with righteousness; the mind of the mean man is conversant with gain.
author: Confucius

text: The mechanic, who wishes to do his work well, must first sharpen his tools.
author: Confucius

text: See what a man does... How can a man conceal his character?
author: Confucius

text: There are three things of which the superior man stands in awe. He stands in awe of the ordinances of Heaven. He stands in awe of great men. He stands in awe of the words of sages.
author: Confucius

text: A minister, in serving his prince, reverently discharges his duties, and makes his emolument a secondary consideration.
author: Confucius

text: When a person does not transgress the boundary line in the great virtues, he may pass and repass it in the small virtues.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zixia (Tsze-hsia)

text: In hearing litigations, I am like any other body. What is necessary, however, is to cause the people to have no litigations.
author: Confucius

text: The superior man is affable, but not adulatory; the mean man is adulatory, but not affable.
author: Confucius

text: The wise are free from perplexities; the virtuous from anxiety; and the bold from fear.
author: Confucius

text: The man, who in the view of gain, thinks of righteousness; who in the view of danger is prepared to give up his life; and who does not forget an old agreement however far back it extends: such a man may be reckoned a COMPLETE man.
author: Confucius

text: The Master, by orderly method, skilfully leads men on. He enlarged my mind with learning, and taught me the restraints of propriety.
author: Confucius
speaker: Yan Hui (Yen Yuan)

text: The father conceals the misconduct of the son, and the son conceals the misconduct of the father. Uprightness is to be found in this.
author: Confucius

text: To rule a country of a thousand chariots, there must be reverent attention to business, and sincerity; economy in expenditure, and love for men; and the employment of the people at the proper seasons.
author: Confucius

text: The officer, having discharged all his duties, should devote his leisure to learning. The student, having completed his learning, should apply himself to be an officer.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zixia (Tsze-hsia)

text: Is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters?
author: Confucius

text: When his knowledge is sufficient to attain, and he has virtue enough to hold fast, if he cannot govern with dignity, the people will not respect him.
author: Confucius

text: When a prince's personal conduct is correct, his government is effective without the issuing of orders. If his personal conduct is not correct, he may issue orders, but they will not be followed.
author: Confucius

text: It is impossible to associate with birds and beasts, as if they were the same with us. If I associate not with these people, with mankind, with whom shall I associate?
author: Confucius

text: I daily examine myself on three points: whether, in transacting business for others, I may have been not faithful; whether, in intercourse with friends, I may have been not sincere; whether I may have not mastered and practised the instructions of my teacher.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zengzi (the philosopher Tsang)

text: Let your evinced desires be for what is good, and the people will be good. The relation between superiors and inferiors, is like that between the wind and the grass. The grass must bend, when the wind blows across it.
author: Confucius

text: Raise to office those whom you know. As to those whom you do not know, will others neglect them?
author: Confucius

text: The firm, the enduring, the simple, and the modest are near to virtue.
author: Confucius

text: When a man feels the difficulty of doing, can he be other than cautious and slow in speaking?
author: Confucius

text: Tsze-lu asked how a ruler should be served. The Master said, 'Do not impose on him, and, moreover, withstand him to his face.'
author: Confucius

text: When the man of high station is well instructed, he loves men; when the man of low station is well instructed, he is easily ruled.
author: Confucius
speaker: Ziyou (Tsze-yu), quoting Confucius

text: The superior man, in the world, does not set his mind either for anything, or against anything; what is right he will follow.
author: Confucius

text: The superior man has a dignified ease without pride. The mean man has pride without a dignified ease.
author: Confucius

text: He was of an active nature and yet fond of learning, and he was not ashamed to ask and learn of his inferiors!
author: Confucius

text: In ancient times, men learned with a view to their own improvement. Now-a-days, men learn with a view to the approbation of others.
author: Confucius

text: Since they are thus numerous, what more shall be done for them?' 'Enrich them,' was the reply.... 'And when they have been enriched, what more shall be done?' The Master said, 'Teach them.'
author: Confucius

text: They will do; but they are not equal to him, who, though poor, is yet cheerful, and to him, who, though rich, loves the rules of propriety.
author: Confucius

text: Mechanics have their shops to dwell in, in order to accomplish their works. The superior man learns, in order to reach to the utmost of his principles.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zixia (Tsze-hsia)

text: There are three things which the superior man guards against. In youth, when the physical powers are not yet settled, he guards against lust. When he is strong and the physical powers are full of vigor, he guards against quarrelsomeness. When he is old, and the animal powers are decayed, he guards against covetousness.
author: Confucius

text: To subdue one's self and return to propriety, is perfect virtue. If a man can for one day subdue himself and return to propriety, all under heaven will ascribe perfect virtue to him. Is the practice of perfect virtue from a man himself, or is it from others?
author: Confucius

text: Every one calls his son his son, whether he has talents or has not talents.
author: Confucius

text: Is he not a man of complete virtue, who feels no discomposure though men may take no note of him?
author: Confucius

text: When agreements are made according to what is right, what is spoken can be made good. When respect is shown according to what is proper, one keeps far from shame and disgrace.
author: Confucius
speaker: Youzi (the philosopher Yu)

text: When the person in authority is beneficent without great expenditure; when he lays tasks on the people without their repining; when he pursues what he desires without being covetous; when he maintains a dignified ease without being proud; when he is majestic without being fierce.
author: Confucius

text: He who speaks without modesty will find it difficult to make his words good.
author: Confucius

text: What the superior man requires, is just that in his words there may be nothing incorrect.
author: Confucius

text: The superior man is distressed by his want of ability. He is not distressed by men's not knowing him.
author: Confucius

text: If, in serving his parents, he can exert his utmost strength; if, in serving his prince, he can devote his life; if, in his intercourse with his friends, his words are sincere: although men say that he has not learned, I will certainly say that he has.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zixia (Tsze-hsia)

text: A man can enlarge the principles which he follows; those principles do not enlarge the man.
author: Confucius

text: The faults of the superior man are like the eclipses of the sun and moon. He has his faults, and all men see them; he changes again, and all men look up to him.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zigong (Tsze-kung)

text: Alas! Your words, sir, show you to be a superior man, but four horses cannot overtake the tongue.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zigong (Tsze-kung)

text: In his conduct of himself, he was humble; in serving his superiors, he was respectful; in nourishing the people, he was kind; in ordering the people, he was just.
author: Confucius

text: There is the love of being benevolent without the love of learning; the beclouding here leads to a foolish simplicity. There is the love of knowing without the love of learning; the beclouding here leads to dissipation of mind.
author: Confucius

text: This man seldom speaks; when he does, he is sure to hit the point.
author: Confucius

text: He who in his conduct of himself maintains a sense of shame, and when sent to any quarter will not disgrace his prince's commission, deserves to be called an officer.
author: Confucius

text: Respectfulness, without the rules of propriety, becomes laborious bustle; carefulness, without the rules of propriety, becomes timidity; boldness, without the rules of propriety, becomes insubordination; straightforwardness, without the rules of propriety, becomes rudeness.
author: Confucius

text: The virtuous will be sure to speak correctly, but those whose speech is good may not always be virtuous. Men of principle are sure to be bold, but those who are bold may not always be men of principle.
author: Confucius

text: At fifteen, I had my mind bent on learning... At seventy, I could follow what my heart desired, without transgressing what was right.
author: Confucius

text: By his generosity, he won all. By his sincerity, he made the people repose trust in him. By his earnest activity, his achievements were great. By his justice, all were delighted.
author: Confucius

text: When those who are in high stations perform well all their duties to their relations, the people are aroused to virtue. When old friends are not neglected by them, the people are preserved from meanness.
author: Confucius

text: Now the man of perfect virtue, wishing to be established himself, seeks also to establish others; wishing to be enlarged himself, he seeks also to enlarge others.
author: Confucius

text: To assail one's own wickedness and not assail that of others; is not this the way to correct cherished evil? For a morning's anger to disregard one's own life, and involve that of his parents; is not this a case of delusion?
author: Confucius

text: High station filled without indulgent generosity; ceremonies performed without reverence; mourning conducted without sorrow; wherewith should I contemplate such ways?
author: Confucius

text: When a bird is about to die, its notes are mournful; when a man is about to die, his words are good.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zengzi (the philosopher Tsang)

text: He, who from day to day recognises what he has not yet, and from month to month does not forget what he has attained to, may be said indeed to love to learn.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zixia (Tsze-hsia)

text: I should like, having chariots and horses, and light fur dresses, to share them with my friends, and though they should spoil them, I would not be displeased.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zilu (Tsze-lu)

text: The difficulty is with the countenance. If, when their elders have any troublesome affairs, the young take the toil of them, and if, when the young have wine and food, they set them before their elders, is THIS to be considered filial piety?
author: Confucius

text: In serving his parents, a son may remonstrate with them, but gently; when he sees that they do not incline to follow his advice, he shows an increased degree of reverence, but does not abandon his purpose; and should they punish him, he does not allow himself to murmur.
author: Confucius

text: Gravity, generosity of soul, sincerity, earnestness, and kindness. If you are grave, you will not be treated with disrespect. If you are generous, you will win all. If you are sincere, people will repose trust in you. If you are earnest, you will accomplish much. If you are kind, this will enable you to employ the services of others.
author: Confucius

text: When rulers love to observe the rules of propriety, the people respond readily to the calls on them for service.
author: Confucius

text: The years of parents may by no means not be kept in the memory, as an occasion at once for joy and for fear.
author: Confucius

text: To conceal resentment against a person, and appear friendly with him; Tso Ch'iu-ming was ashamed of such conduct. I also am ashamed of it.
author: Confucius

text: It is, in retirement, to be sedately grave; in the management of business, to be reverently attentive; in intercourse with others, to be strictly sincere. Though a man go among rude, uncultivated tribes, these qualities may not be neglected.
author: Confucius

text: It is, when you go abroad, to behave to every one as if you were receiving a great guest; to employ the people as if you were assisting at a great sacrifice; not to do to others as you would not wish done to yourself; to have no murmuring against you in the country, and none in the family.
author: Confucius

text: Tsze-lu never slept over a promise.
author: Confucius

text: The superior man honours the talented and virtuous, and bears with all. He praises the good, and pities the incompetent.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zizhang (Tsze-chang)

text: He who requires much from himself and little from others, will keep himself from being the object of resentment.
author: Confucius

text: With coarse rice to eat, with water to drink, and my bended arm for a pillow; I have still joy in the midst of these things. Riches and honours acquired by unrighteousness, are to me as a floating cloud.
author: Confucius

text: He who puts on an appearance of stern firmness, while inwardly he is weak, is like one of the small, mean people; yea, is he not like the thief who breaks through, or climbs over, a wall?
author: Confucius

text: When good government prevails in a state, to be thinking only of salary; and, when bad government prevails, to be thinking, in the same way, only of salary; this is shameful.
author: Confucius

text: Having not and yet affecting to have, empty and yet affecting to be full, straitened and yet affecting to be at ease: it is difficult with such characteristics to have constancy.
author: Confucius

text: The Master said, 'The cautious seldom err.'
author: Confucius

text: The officer may not be without breadth of mind and vigorous endurance. His burden is heavy and his course is long.
author: Confucius
speaker: Zengzi (the philosopher Tsang)

text: The wise find pleasure in water; the virtuous find pleasure in hills. The wise are active; the virtuous are tranquil. The wise are joyful; the virtuous are long-lived.
author: Confucius

text: From of old, death has been the lot of all men; but if the people have no faith in their rulers, there is no standing for the state.
author: Confucius

text: When the multitude hate a man, it is necessary to examine into the case. When the multitude like a man, it is necessary to examine into the case.
author: Confucius

text: Riches and honours are what men desire. If it cannot be obtained in the proper way, they should not be held.
