text: Men can endure to hear others praised only so long as they can severally persuade themselves of their own ability to equal the actions recounted: when this point is passed, envy comes in and with it incredulity.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Pericles

text: Those of course who have a free choice in the matter and whose fortunes are not at stake, war is the greatest of follies. But if the only choice was between submission with loss of independence, and danger with the hope of preserving that independence, in such a case it is he who will not accept the risk that deserves blame, not he who will.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Pericles

text: Indeed sensible men are prudent enough to treat their gains as precarious, just as they would also keep a clear head in adversity, and think that war, so far from staying within the limit to which a combatant may wish to confine it, will run the course that its chances prescribe;
author: Thucydides
speaker: The Lacedaemonian envoys

text: In peace and prosperity, states and individuals have better sentiments, because they do not find themselves suddenly confronted with imperious necessities; but war takes away the easy supply of daily wants, and so proves a rough master, that brings most men's characters to a level with their fortunes.
author: Thucydides

text: If we undertake the war without preparation, we should by hastening its commencement only delay its conclusion:
author: Thucydides
speaker: Archidamus

text: The most alarming feature in the case is the constant change of measures with which we appear to be threatened, and our seeming ignorance of the fact that bad laws which are never changed are better for a city than good ones that have no authority; that unlearned loyalty is more serviceable than quick-witted insubordination; and that ordinary men usually manage public affairs better than their more gifted fellows.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Cleon

text: We know that the fortune of war is sometimes more impartial than the disproportion of numbers might lead one to suppose; to submit is to give ourselves over to despair, while action still preserves for us a hope that we may stand erect.
author: Thucydides
speaker: The Melians

text: Indeed if great enmities are ever to be really settled, we think it will be, not by the system of revenge and military success, and by forcing an opponent to swear to a treaty to his disadvantage, but when the more fortunate combatant waives these his privileges, to be guided by gentler feelings conquers his rival in generosity, and accords peace on more moderate conditions than he expected.
author: Thucydides
speaker: The Lacedaemonian envoys

text: Vengeance is not necessarily successful because wrong has been done, or strength sure because it is confident; but the incalculable element in the future exercises the widest influence, and is the most treacherous, and yet in fact the most useful of all things, as it frightens us all equally, and thus makes us consider before attacking each other.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Hermocrates

text: The ancient simplicity into which honour so largely entered was laughed down and disappeared; and society became divided into camps in which no man trusted his fellow.
author: Thucydides

text: No one can quarrel with a people for making, in matters of tremendous risk, the best provision that it can for its interest.
author: Thucydides
speaker: The Athenian envoys

text: In generosity we are equally singular, acquiring our friends by conferring, not by receiving, favours. Yet, of course, the doer of the favour is the firmer friend of the two, in order by continued kindness to keep the recipient in his debt; while the debtor feels less keenly from the very consciousness that the return he makes will be a payment, not a free gift.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Pericles

text: We cultivate refinement without extravagance and knowledge without effeminacy; wealth we employ more for use than for show, and place the real disgrace of poverty not in owning to the fact but in declining the struggle against it.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Pericles

text: Take time then in forming your resolution, as the matter is of great importance; and do not be persuaded by the opinions and complaints of others to bring trouble on yourselves, but consider the vast influence of accident in war, before you are engaged in it. As it continues, it generally becomes an affair of chances, chances from which neither of us is exempt, and whose event we must risk in the dark. It is a common mistake in going to war to begin at the wrong end, to act first, and wait for disaster to discuss the matter.
author: Thucydides
speaker: The Athenian envoys

text: Indeed men too often take upon themselves in the prosecution of their revenge to set the example of doing away with those general laws to which all alike can look for salvation in adversity, instead of allowing them to subsist against the day of danger when their aid may be required.
author: Thucydides

text: instead of looking on discussion as a stumbling-block in the way of action, we think it an indispensable preliminary to any wise action at all.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Pericles

text: For heroes have the whole earth for their tomb; and in lands far from their own, where the column with its epitaph declares it, there is enshrined in every breast a record unwritten with no tablet to preserve it, except that of the heart.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Pericles

text: Hope, danger's comforter, may be indulged in by those who have abundant resources, if not without loss at all events without ruin; but its nature is to be extravagant, and those who go so far as to put their all upon the venture see it in its true colours only when they are ruined; but so long as the discovery would enable them to guard against it, it is never found wanting.
author: Thucydides
speaker: The Athenian envoys at Melos

text: You, Lacedaemonians, of all the Hellenes are alone inactive, and defend yourselves not by doing anything but by looking as if you would do something; you alone wait till the power of an enemy is becoming twice its original size, instead of crushing it in its infancy.
author: Thucydides
speaker: The Corinthian envoys

text: the safest rule of life is to take one's character and institutions for better and for worse, and to live up to them as closely as one can.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Alcibiades

text: The Lacedaemonians meanwhile, man to man, and with their war-songs in the ranks, exhorted each brave comrade to remember what he had learnt before; well aware that the long training of action was of more saving virtue than any brief verbal exhortation, though never so well delivered.
author: Thucydides

text: From that moment, instead of the debt of revenge which violence must entail, his adversary owes a debt of generosity to be paid in kind, and is inclined by honour to stand to his agreement. And men oftener act in this manner towards their greatest enemies than where the quarrel is of less importance; they are also by nature as glad to give way to those who first yield to them, as they are apt to be provoked by arrogance to risks condemned by their own judgment.
author: Thucydides
speaker: The Lacedaemonian envoys

text: There is, however, no advantage in reflections on the past further than may be of service to the present.
author: Thucydides
speaker: The Corinthian envoys

text: The palm of courage will surely be adjudged most justly to those, who best know the difference between hardship and pleasure and yet are never tempted to shrink from danger.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Pericles

text: Yet in justice the same cases should be decided in the same way, and policy should not mean anything else than lasting gratitude for the service of good ally combined with a proper attention to one's own immediate interest.
author: Thucydides
speaker: The Plataeans

text: If wise men remain quiet, while they are not injured, brave men abandon peace for war when they are injured, returning to an understanding on a favourable opportunity: in fact, they are neither intoxicated by their success in war, nor disposed to take an injury for the sake of the delightful tranquillity of peace.
author: Thucydides
speaker: The Corinthian envoys

text: you can avoid the mistake of those who meet with an extraordinary piece of good fortune, and are led on by hope to grasp continually at something further, through having already succeeded without expecting it. While those who have known most vicissitudes of good and bad, have also justly least faith in their prosperity; and to teach your city and ours this lesson experience has not been wanting.
author: Thucydides
speaker: The Lacedaemonian envoys

text: That war is an evil is a proposition so familiar to every one that it would be tedious to develop it. No one is forced to engage in it by ignorance, or kept out of it by fear, if he fancies there is anything to be gained by it. To the former the gain appears greater than the danger, while the latter would rather stand the risk than put up with any immediate sacrifice.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Hermocrates

text: For the only light in which you can view their land is that of a hostage in your hands, a hostage the more valuable the better it is cultivated. This you ought to spare as long as possible, and not make them desperate, and so increase the difficulty of dealing with them.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Archidamus

text: If many ill-conceived plans have succeeded through the still greater fatuity of an opponent, many more, apparently well laid, have on the contrary ended in disgrace. The confidence with which we form our schemes is never completely justified in their execution; speculation is carried on in safety, but, when it comes to action, fear causes failure.
author: Thucydides
speaker: The Corinthian envoys

text: what an intending ally trusts to is not the goodwill of those who ask his aid, but a decided superiority of power for action;
author: Thucydides
speaker: The Athenian envoys at Melos

text: If you give way, you will instantly have to meet some greater demand, as having been frightened into obedience in the first instance; while a firm refusal will make them clearly understand that they must treat you more as equals.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Pericles

text: Hatred and unpopularity at the moment have fallen to the lot of all who have aspired to rule others; but where odium must be incurred, true wisdom incurs it for the highest objects. Hatred also is short-lived; but that which makes the splendour of the present and the glory of the future remains for ever unforgotten.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Pericles

text: In practice we always base our preparations against an enemy on the assumption that his plans are good; indeed, it is right to rest our hopes not on a belief in his blunders, but on the soundness of our provisions. Nor ought we to believe that there is much difference between man and man, but to think that the superiority lies with him who is reared in the severest school.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Archidamus

text: A man ought, therefore, to consider these points, and not to think of running risks with a country placed so critically, or of grasping at another empire before we have secured the one we have already;
author: Thucydides
speaker: Nicias

text: Let us not shrink from the risk, but let us remember that this is just the occasion for one of the baseless panics common in war: and that to be able to guard against these in one's own case, and to detect the moment when an attack will find an enemy at this disadvantage, is what makes a successful general.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Teutiaplus

text: The most successful soldier will always be the man who most happily detects a blunder like this, and who carefully consulting his own means makes his attack not so much by open and regular approaches, as by seizing the opportunity of the moment; and these stratagems, which do the greatest service to our friends by most completely deceiving our enemies, have the most brilliant name in war.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Brasidas

text: It must be thoroughly understood that war is a necessity; but that the more readily we accept it, the less will be the ardour of our opponents, and that out of the greatest dangers communities and individuals acquire the greatest glory.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Pericles

text: For the most part, where there is the greatest hope, there is also the greatest ardour for action.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Gylippus and the Syracusan generals

text: I hope that none of you in our present strait will think to show his wit by exactly calculating all the perils that encompass us, but that you will rather hasten to close with the enemy, without staying to count the odds, seeing in this your best chance of safety. In emergencies like ours calculation is out of place; the sooner the danger is faced the better.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Demosthenes

text: That the Athenians should cherish this ambition and practise this policy is very excusable; and I do not blame those who wish to rule, but those who are over-ready to serve. It is just as much in men's nature to rule those who submit to them, as it is to resist those who molest them; one is not less invariable than the other.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Hermocrates

text: The hand of heaven must be borne with resignation, that of the enemy with fortitude;
author: Thucydides
speaker: Pericles

text: An adversary numerically superior, like the one before us, comes into action trusting more to strength than to resolution; while he who voluntarily confronts tremendous odds must have very great internal resources to draw upon.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Phormio

text: Praise is due to all who, if not so superior to human nature as to refuse dominion, yet respect justice more than their position compels them to do.
author: Thucydides
speaker: The Athenian envoys

text: Without equal military strength it was impossible to contribute equal or fair counsel to the common interest.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Themistocles

text: A man may be personally ever so well off, and yet if his country be ruined he must be ruined with it; whereas a flourishing commonwealth always affords chances of salvation to unfortunate individuals.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Pericles

text: Men's minds are affected by what they hear, and besides the first to attack, or to show that they mean to defend themselves against an attack, inspire greater fear because men see that they are ready for the emergency.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Hermocrates

text: For kindness opportunely shown has a greater power of removing old grievances than the facts of the case may warrant.
author: Thucydides
speaker: The Corinthian envoys

text: since they whose minds are least sensitive to calamity, and whose hands are most quick to meet it, are the greatest men and the greatest communities.
author: Thucydides
speaker: Pericles

text: Whilst mother remains, one son is cold; if mother departs, three sons will be destitute.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Min Sun
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)

text: If the head of a family do not act haughtily towards his servant, he cannot act so to his wife and children. Hence he will gain the goodwill of all his people, and they will help him in the fulfilment of his filial duty.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter VIII, Filial Duty in Government

text: A filial son has five duties to perform to his parents: (1) He must venerate them in daily life. (2) He must try to make them happy in every possible way, especially when the meal is served. (3) He must take extra care of them when they are sick. (4) He ought to show great sorrow for them when they are dead. (5) He must offer sacrifices to his deceased parents with the utmost solemnity.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter X, The Filial Duty of a Son

text: Be careful as though you were standing upon the brink of a high precipice or treading on thin ice.

speaker: Quoted from the Shih Ching
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter III, The Filial Duty of Feudal Princes

text: Our body and hair and skin are all derived from our parents, and therefore we have no right to injure any of them in the least. This is the first duty of a child.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)

text: The feeling of affection is fostered during the time of infancy, and from that affection springs reverence.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter IX, Government by the Sage

text: You must think of your ancestors and continue to cultivate the virtue which you inherit from them.

speaker: Confucius, quoting the Ta Ya
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter I, The Meaning of Filial Duty

text: In order to prevent the people from treating their parents with cruelty, the Emperor first sets an example to them by showing a dear love to his mother; and in order to teach them not to treat their parents with rudeness, he first treats his parents with respect.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter II, The Filial Duty of an Emperor

text: To live an upright life and to spread the great doctrines of humanity must win good reputation after death, and reflect great honour upon our parents. This is the last duty of a son.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter I, The Meaning of Filial Duty

text: When the command is wrong, a son should resist his father, and a minister should resist his August Master.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter XV, The Question of Remonstrance

text: When his parents are in error, the son must remonstrate with them with respect and gently. If they do not receive his reproof, he must strive more and more to be dutiful and respectful towards them till they are pleased, and then he must again point out their fault.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Quoted from the Li Chi (Book of Rites)
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Introduction, III. Filial Duty and Parental Love

text: If he is proud and haughty when he is a high official, he will soon bring ruin upon himself and his family; if he feels dissatisfied with his lower position, he may be led to do illegal acts; and if he does anything contrary to the public feeling, he will probably be the object of attacks.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter X, The Filial Duty of a Son

text: He always shows reverence to his elder brothers, and in order to fulfil his duty to them to the fullest extent, he does the same towards every one who is older than he.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter XIV, Amplification of Raising the Reputation

text: When a ruler wishes to teach his people to love their parents, he does not go to their family every day to teach them. He teaches them by his showing reverence to all old people.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter XIII, Amplification of The Highest Virtue

text: Do not do anything in the course of a day which will reflect dishonour upon your ancestors.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Quoted from the Shih Ching
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter V, The Filial Duty of the Literary Class

text: The duty of children to their parents is the fountain whence all other virtues spring, and also the starting-point from which we ought to begin our education.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter I, The Meaning of Filial Duty

text: The best way to teach the people to love their sovereign is for the sovereign first to love his own parents; to teach them to be polite to each other is for the sovereign himself first to be polite to all his elders.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter XII, Amplification of the Important Doctrine

text: Any man will be secure in his position, however high it may be, if he does not behave himself in a haughty manner; and will be ever able to keep his wealth if he is frugal and careful in his expenses.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter III, The Filial Duty of Feudal Princes

text: The maxim is, 'Resist when wrongly commanded.' Hence how can he be called filial who obeys his father when he is commanded to do wrong?
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter XV, The Question of Remonstrance

text: There is nothing so great in the world as man, and there is nothing so great in a man as filial piety.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter IX, Government by the Sage

text: If you adorn yourself with the highest virtue, the whole world will follow you.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Quoted from the Shih Ching
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter VIII, Filial Duty in Government

text: The first duty of a son is to pay a careful attention to every want of his parents. The next is to serve his government loyally; and the last to establish a good name for himself.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter I, The Meaning of Filial Duty

text: Am I to punish for a breach of filial piety one who has never been taught to be filially minded? Is not he who neglects to teach his son his duties equally guilty with the son who fails in them?
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Introduction, III. Filial Duty and Parental Love

text: They made every person love his parents by loving their own parents first. They induced every person to cultivate his virtue by expounding the advantages of virtue to him. They behaved themselves respectfully and humbly, so that the people might not quarrel with one another.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)

text: When wives and children and their sires are one, 'Tis like the harp and lute in unison. When brothers live in concord and in peace, The strains of harmony shall never cease.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Quoted from the Book of Odes
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Introduction, III. Filial Duty and Parental Love

text: Having thus wronged himself, he cannot be considered as a filial son, although he treats his parents every day to luxurious meals.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter X, The Filial Duty of a Son

text: If such persons are rulers of a state, they will afford to the people a good example to follow and will also inspire them with reverence and affection.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter IX, Government by the Sage

text: Any one who gets a high position, such as that of a ruler, by undue influence instead of by good actions, will be despised by good men. As to the latter, they say what they ought to say, and do what they think is good for the public.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter IX, Government by the Sage

text: What is etiquette? It is simply due respect to one's elders. If I respect the parents, the son will be pleased; if I respect the elder brothers, the younger ones will be pleased; and if I respect the sovereign, all the ministers will be pleased.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter XII, Amplification of the Important Doctrine

text: Why do we offer sacrifices to our ancestors in our family shrine? Because we ought not to forget them. Why must we cultivate our minds and be circumspect in our actions? Because we do not wish to bring disgrace upon the name of our ancestors.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter XVI, The Influence and Fruit of Filial Piety

text: Children should have deep and ardent affection for their parents, who have endured so much anxiety in nourishing them.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Quoted from the Book of Odes
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)

text: When our parents are alive, we should treat them with love and respect. When they are dead, we should have sorrow for them. By doing so we shall have performed the duty of mankind, and have done what ought to be done by a filial son, and by the living to the dead.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter XVIII, Mourning for One's Parents

text: Filial duty is the constant doctrine of Heaven, the natural righteousness of Earth, and the practical duty of man. Every member of the community ought to observe it with the greatest care.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)

text: From the Emperor downwards to the common people, every one has the same duty imposed upon him, and there is no instance in which we can find that a man cannot fulfil this duty.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter VI, The Filial Duty of Common People

text: He will carry out any praiseworthy schemes projected by his master, and will correct any fault which he may commit. In this way a great affection will be fostered between them.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)

text: As he can maintain order in his family affairs, so he can do the same in the government. He bases the principle of the government of a State upon that of a ruling family, and the consequent success will make his name to be remembered throughout generations to come.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter XIV, Amplification of Raising the Reputation

text: If a man has a good friend to resist him in doing bad actions, he will have his reputation preserved; so if a father has a son to resist his wrong commands, he will be saved from committing serious faults.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
speaker: Confucius
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter XV, The Question of Remonstrance

text: Having loved and respected his own parents, his good conduct will influence the minds of his people, and his good example will be followed by them.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter II, The Filial Duty of an Emperor

text: From the manner in which we should treat our father we learn how to treat our mother. The love toward them is the same.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter V, The Filial Duty of the Literary Class

text: To do the necessary in every season (such as growing crops in spring and reaping harvest in autumn), to do the utmost to make lands as fertile as possible, and to be frugal in their expense, in order to keep their parents in comfort, is the filial duty of the common people.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter VI, The Filial Duty of Common People

text: When an Emperor can live in harmony with his elders, there will be harmony throughout his dominion between superiors and inferiors.
author: Confucius and Zengzi
reference: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiao Jing)
locator: Chapter XVI, The Influence and Fruit of Filial Piety

text: In this way though he has his place above them, men do not feel his weight, nor though he has his place before them, do they feel it an injury to them.

text: I have three precious things which I prize and hold fast. The first is gentleness; the second is economy; and the third is shrinking from taking precedence of others.
author: Laozi

text: The great state only wishes to unite men together and nourish them; a small state only wishes to be received by, and to serve, the other. Each gets what it desires, but the great state must learn to abase itself.

text: Who can (make) the muddy water (clear)? Let it be still, and it will gradually become clear. Who can secure the condition of rest? Let movement go on, and the condition of rest will gradually arise.

text: For regulating the human (in our constitution) and rendering the (proper) service to the heavenly, there is nothing like moderation.

text: The Tao in its regular course does nothing (for the sake of doing it), and so there is nothing which it does not do.

text: Every one in the world knows that the soft overcomes the hard, and the weak the strong, but no one is able to carry it out in practice.
author: Laozi

text: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends. Clay is fashioned into vessels; but it is on their empty hollowness, that their use depends.
author: Laozi

text: The sage does not accumulate (for himself). The more that he expends for others, the more does he possess of his own; the more that he gives to others, the more does he have himself.
author: Laozi

text: The great Tao (or way) is very level and easy; but people love the by-ways.
author: Laozi

text: He is free from self-display, and therefore he shines; from self-assertion, and therefore he is distinguished; from self-boasting, and therefore his merit is acknowledged; from self-complacency, and therefore he acquires superiority. It is because he is thus free from striving that therefore no one in the world is able to strive with him.
author: Laozi

text: Calm and repose are what he prizes; victory (by force of arms) is to him undesirable. To consider this desirable would be to delight in the slaughter of men; and he who delights in the slaughter of men cannot get his will in the kingdom.
author: Laozi

text: Who thinks his great achievements poor Shall find his vigour long endure.
author: Laozi

text: To consider what is small as great, and a few as many; and to recompense injury with kindness.
author: Laozi

author: Aristotle

author: Aristotle

text: Hast thou children? instruct them, and bow down their neck from their youth.

text: In three things I was beautified, and stood up beautiful both before God and men: the unity of brethren, the love of neighbours, a man and a wife that agree together.

text: A faithfull friend is a strong defence: and he that hath found such an one hath found a treasure.... Nothing doth countervail a faithful friend, and his excellency is invaluable.

text: There is that for bashfulness promiseth to his friend, and maketh him his enemy for nothing.

text: Forsake not an old friend; for the new is not comparable to him: a new friend is as new wine; when it is old, thou shalt drink it with pleasure.

text: I will not be ashamed to defend a friend; neither will I hide myself from him.

text: Brethren and help are against time of trouble: but alms shall deliver more than them both.

text: A wise man will hold his tongue till he see opportunity: but a babbler and a fool will regard no time.

text: Be not hasty in thy tongue, and in thy deeds slack and remiss.

text: Be faithful to thy neighbour in his poverty, that thou mayest rejoice in his prosperity: abide stedfast unto him in the time of his trouble, that thou mayest be heir with him in his heritage: for a mean estate is not always to be contemned: nor the rich that is foolish to be had in admiration.

text: Abstain from strife, and thou shalt diminish thy sins: for a furious man will kindle strife... A sinful man disquieteth friends, and maketh debate among them that be at peace.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Judge not thy neighbour by thyself: and be discreet in every point.

text: Whoso honoureth his father maketh an atonement for his sins... He that honoureth his mother is as one that layeth up treasure.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: If thou hast opened thy mouth against thy friend, fear not; for there may be a reconciliation: except for upbraiding, or pride, or disclosing of secrets, or a treacherous wound: for these things every friend will depart.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Honour thy father and mother both in word and deed, that a blessing may come upon thee from them.... The blessing of the father establisheth the houses of children; but the curse of the mother rooteth out foundations.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: The stroke of the whip maketh marks in the flesh: but the stroke of the tongue breaketh the bones.... Many have fallen by the edge of the sword: but not so many as have fallen by the tongue.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: As the sun when it ariseth in the high heaven; so is the beauty of a good wife in the ordering of her house.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: O how comely is the wisdom of old men, and understanding and counsel to men of honour.... Much experience is the crown of old men, and the fear of God is their glory.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: A wise man by his words maketh him beloved: but the graces of fools shall be poured out.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Honour and shame is in talk: and the tongue of man is his fall.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: If thou wouldest get a friend, prove him first and be not hasty to credit him.... Some man is a friend for his own occasion, and will not abide in the day of thy trouble.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Chastise thy son, and hold him to labour, lest his lewd behaviour be an offence unto thee.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: It is much better to reprove, than to be angry secretly: and he that confesseth his fault shall be preserved from hurt.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: A wise judge will instruct his people; and the government of a prudent man is well ordered.... As the judge of the people is himself, so are his officers; and what manner of man the ruler of the city is, such are all they that dwell therein.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Rehearse not unto another that which is told unto thee, and thou shalt fare never the worse.... Whether it be to friend or foe, talk not of other men's lives; and if thou canst without offence, reveal them not.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Curse the whisperer and doubletongued: for such have destroyed many that were at peace.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: A wise man instructeth his people; and the fruits of his understanding fail not.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Make not thyself an underling to a foolish man; neither accept the person of the mighty.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Let reason go before every enterprize, and counsel before every action.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Dishonour not a man in his old age: for even some of us wax old.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Rejoice not over thy greatest enemy being dead, but remember that we die all.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Every counsellor extolleth counsel; but there is some that counselleth for himself.... Beware of a counsellor, and know before what need he hath; for he will counsel for himself; lest he cast the lot upon thee.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: If thou be among the indiscreet, observe the time; but be continually among men of understanding.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Help thy neighbour according to thy power, and beware that thou thyself fall not into the same.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: An unwise king destroyeth his people; but through the prudence of them which are in authority the city shall be inhabited.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: My son, go on with thy business in meekness; so shalt thou be beloved of him that is approved.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Lose thy money for thy brother and thy friend, and let it not rust under a stone to be lost.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: If children live honestly, and have wherewithal, they shall cover the baseness of their parents.... Children, being haughty, through disdain and want of nurture do stain the nobility of their kindred.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: A faithful friend is the medicine of life; and they that fear the Lord shall find him.... Whoso feareth the Lord shall direct his friendship aright: for as he is, so shall his neighbour be also.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Though his father die, yet he is as though he were not dead: for he hath left one behind him that is like himself.... While he lived, he saw and rejoiced in him: and when he died, he was not sorrowful.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Get thyself the love of the congregation, and bow thy head to a great man.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Seek not to be judge, being not able to take away iniquity; lest at any time thou fear the person of the mighty, an stumblingblock in the way of thy uprightness.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: A friend and companion never meet amiss: but above both is a wife with her husband.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Travel not by the way with a bold fellow, lest he become grievous unto thee: for he will do according to his own will, and thou shalt perish with him through his folly.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Deliver him that suffereth wrong from the hand of the oppressor; and be not fainthearted when thou sittest in judgment.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: He that toucheth pitch shall be defiled therewith; and he that hath fellowship with a proud man shall be like unto him.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: The fruit declareth if the tree have been dressed; so is the utterance of a conceit in the heart of man.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Separate thyself from thine enemies, and take heed of thy friends.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Sweet language will multiply friends: and a fairspeaking tongue will increase kind greetings.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Commend not a man for his beauty; neither abhor a man for his outward appearance.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Laugh no man to scorn in the bitterness of his soul: for there is one which humbleth and exalteth.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: As near as thou canst, guess at thy neighbour, and consult with the wise.... Let thy talk be with the wise, and all thy communication in the law of the most High.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Be in peace with many: nevertheless have but one counsellor of a thousand.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: If thou blow the spark, it shall burn: if thou spit upon it, it shall be quenched: and both these come out of thy mouth.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: He that teacheth his son grieveth the enemy: and before his friends he shall rejoice of him.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: He that getteth a wife beginneth a possession, a help like unto himself, and a pillar of rest.... Where no hedge is, there the possession is spoiled: and he that hath no wife will wander up and down mourning.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: An honest man is surety for his neighbour: but he that is impudent will forsake him.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: An horse not broken becometh headstrong: and a child left to himself will be wilful.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Make not an hungry soul sorrowful; neither provoke a man in his distress.... Add not more trouble to an heart that is vexed; and defer not to give to him that is in need.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: If thou have a servant, entreat him as a brother: for thou hast need of him, as of thine own soul: if thou entreat him evil, and he run from thee, which way wilt thou go to seek him?
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Learn before thou speak, and use physick or ever thou be sick.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: If a skilful man hear a wise word, he will commend it, and add unto it: but as soon as one of no understanding heareth it, it displeaseth him, and he casteth it behind his back.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: If a servant say to his master, I will not do as it pleaseth thee; though afterward he do it, he angereth him that nourisheth him.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: There is a companion, which helpeth his friend for the belly, and taketh up the buckler against the enemy.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: The knowledge of a wise man shall abound like a flood: and his counsel is like a pure fountain of life.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: There is one that laboureth, and taketh pains, and maketh haste, and is so much the more behind.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Consult not with a fool; for he cannot keep counsel.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: He that is hasty to give credit is lightminded; and he that sinneth shall offend against his own soul.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: The greater thou art, the more humble thyself, and thou shalt find favour before the Lord.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: If thou be made the master lift not thyself up, but be among them as one of the rest; take diligent care for them, and so sit down.... When thou hast done all thy office, take thy place, that thou mayest be merry with them, and receive a crown for thy well ordering of the feast.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Miss not the discourse of the elders: for they also learned of their fathers, and of them thou shalt learn understanding, and to give answer as need requireth.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Forego not a wise and good woman: for her grace is above gold.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: There is a companion, which rejoiceth in the prosperity of a friend, but in the time of trouble will be against him.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Strive not with a man that is full of tongue, and heap not wood upon his fire.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Presents and gifts blind the eyes of the wise, and stop up his mouth that he cannot reprove.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Remember thy end, and let enmity cease.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Never trust thine enemy: for like as iron rusteth, so is his wickedness.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: An enemy speaketh sweetly with his lips, but in his heart he imagineth how to throw thee into a pit: he will weep with his eyes, but if he find opportunity, he will not be satisfied with blood.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Consult not with one that suspecteth thee: and hide thy counsel from such as envy thee.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Be not excessive toward any; and without discretion do nothing.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: As timber girt and bound together in a building cannot be loosed with shaking: so the heart that is stablished by advised counsel shall fear at no time.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Whatsoever thou takest in hand, remember the end, and thou shalt never do amiss.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Be as a father unto the fatherless, and instead of an husband unto their mother: so shalt thou be as the son of the most High, and he shall love thee more than thy mother doth.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Be swift to hear; and let thy life be sincere; and with patience give answer.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Devise not a lie against thy brother; neither do the like to thy friend.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Because of unrighteous dealings, injuries, and riches got by deceit, the kingdom is translated from one people to another.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: He that chastiseth his son shall have joy in him, and shall rejoice of him among his acquaintance.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Deliver all things in number and weight; and put all in writing that thou givest out, or receivest in.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: A rich man beginning to fall is held up of his friends: but a poor man being down is thrust away by his friends.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Forget not the friendship of thy surety, for he hath given his life for thee.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: My son, help thy father in his age, and grieve him not as long as he liveth.... If his understanding fail, have patience with him; and despise him not when thou art in thy full strength.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: My son, blemish not thy good deeds, neither use uncomfortable words when thou givest any thing.... Shall not the dew asswage the heat? so is a word better than a gift.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: A friend cannot be known in prosperity: and an enemy cannot be hidden in adversity.... In the prosperity of a man enemies will be grieved: but in his adversity even a friend will depart.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: My son, gather instruction from thy youth up: so shalt thou find wisdom till thine old age.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Whoso casteth a stone at the birds frayeth them away: and he that upbraideth his friend breaketh friendship.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Use not many words in a multitude of elders.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Change not a friend for any good by no means; neither a faithful brother for the gold of Ophir.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: He that maketh too much of his son shall bind up his wounds; and his bowels will be troubled at every cry.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: If thou be among great men, make not thyself equal with them; and when ancient men are in place, use not many words.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Forgive thy neighbour the hurt that he hath done unto thee, so shall thy sins also be forgiven when thou prayest.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Open not thine heart to every man, lest he requite thee with a shrewd turn.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: As for a wound, it may be bound up; and after reviling there may be reconcilement: but he that betrayeth secrets is without hope.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: He that requiteth good turns is mindful of that which may come hereafter; and when he falleth, he shall find a stay.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: All these trust to their hands: and every one is wise in his work.... Without these cannot a city be inhabited.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: Lend to thy neighbour in time of his need, and pay thou thy neighbour again in due season.... Keep thy word, and deal faithfully with him, and thou shalt always find the thing that is necessary for thee.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: The heart of fools is in their mouth: but the mouth of the wise is in their heart.
author: Jesus ben Sira

text: There is nothing in which I habitually find greater satisfaction than in the consciousness of serving my friend; and if on any occasion I do not meet with an adequate return, I am not at all sorry to have the balance of kindness in my favour.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
locator: Letter III, to Cn. Pompeius Magnus

text: For I need not say in writing to you, who knows it quite well, how kind and sweet-tempered my brother is, as ready to forgive as he is sensitive in taking offence.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero

text: If you will only make up your mind to believe that the best men are often those whose feelings are most easily irritated and appeased, and that this quickness, so to speak, and sensitiveness of disposition are generally signs of a good heart; and lastly, and this is the main thing, that we must mutually put up with each other's gaucheries (shall I call them?), or faults, or injurious acts, then these misunderstandings will, I hope, be easily smoothed away.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero

text: I am on the threshold, as it were, of a second life. Already certain persons who defended me in my absence begin to nurse a secret grudge at me now that I am here, and to make no secret of their jealousy.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero

text: Men are bound, when writing of themselves, both to speak with greater reserve of what is praiseworthy, and to omit what calls for blame. Added to which such writing carries less conviction, less weight.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero

text: Nothing is better fitted to interest a reader than variety of circumstance and vicissitudes of fortune, which, though the reverse of welcome to us in actual experience, will make very pleasant reading: for the untroubled recollection of a past sorrow has a charm of its own.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero

text: While we all ought in the administration of the state to keep always in view the object I have very frequently mentioned, peace combined with dignity, we are not bound always to use the same language, but to fix our eyes on the same object.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
locator: Letter XV, to P. Lentulus Spinther

text: Such as are the chief men in a republic, such are ever wont to be the other citizens.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
locator: Letter XV, to P. Lentulus Spinther

text: For the persistence in the same view has never been regarded as a merit in men eminent for their guidance of the helm of state; but as in steering a ship one secret of the art is to run before the storm, even if you cannot make the harbour; yet, when you can do so by tacking about, it is folly to keep to the course you have begun rather than by changing it to arrive all the same at the destination you desire.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
locator: Letter XV, to P. Lentulus Spinther

text: My only effort is that I may not fail either my friends or those more remotely connected with me in either active service, or counsel, or personal exertion.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
locator: Letter XV, to P. Lentulus Spinther

text: Maintain a political controversy only so far as you can convince your fellow citizens of its justice: never offer violence to parent or fatherland.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
locator: Letter XV, to P. Lentulus Spinther

text: The rule of Epicharmus, 'Notice how he has treated another.'
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
locator: Letter XIV, to his brother Quintus

text: Ought not the defects of an army to be as carefully concealed as the wounds in our bodies, lest we should increase the enemy's hopes?
author: Julius Caesar
speaker: Curio
reference: Commentaries on the Gallic and Civil Wars
locator: Civil War, Book II, Chapter XXXI
translation: W. A. McDevitte and W. S. Bohn, 1869

text: He knew that in the case of all those whose army had not been obedient to command, either upon some mismanagement of an affair, fortune had deserted them, or, that upon some crime being discovered, covetousness had been clearly proved
author: Julius Caesar
speaker: Caesar
reference: Commentaries on the Gallic and Civil Wars
translation: W. A. McDevitte and W. S. Bohn, 1869

text: It happens, from a common infirmity of human nature, that we are more flushed with confidence, or more vehemently alarmed at things unseen, concealed, and unknown,
author: Julius Caesar
reference: Commentaries on the Gallic and Civil Wars
translation: W. A. McDevitte and W. S. Bohn, 1869

text: From which a judgment might be formed of the advantages which resolution carries with it, inasmuch as those whom for some time they had groundlessly dreaded when unarmed, they had afterwards vanquished, when well armed and flushed with success.
author: Julius Caesar
speaker: Caesar
reference: Commentaries on the Gallic and Civil Wars
translation: W. A. McDevitte and W. S. Bohn, 1869

text: in most cases men willingly believe what they wish.
author: Julius Caesar
reference: Commentaries on the Gallic and Civil Wars
translation: W. A. McDevitte and W. S. Bohn, 1869

text: Here it might be learned how much fortune achieves in war, and how great casualties she produces.
author: Julius Caesar
reference: Commentaries on the Gallic and Civil Wars
translation: W. A. McDevitte and W. S. Bohn, 1869

text: Fortune accomplishes much, not only in other matters, but also in the art of war.
author: Julius Caesar
reference: Commentaries on the Gallic and Civil Wars
translation: W. A. McDevitte and W. S. Bohn, 1869

text: Fortune, who exerts a powerful influence as well in other matters, as especially in war, effects great changes from trifling causes,
author: Julius Caesar
reference: Commentaries on the Gallic and Civil Wars
translation: W. A. McDevitte and W. S. Bohn, 1869

text: To be unable to bear privation for a short time is disgraceful cowardice, not true valour. Those who voluntarily offer themselves to death are more easily found than those who would calmly endure distress.
author: Julius Caesar
speaker: Critognatus
reference: Commentaries on the Gallic and Civil Wars
translation: W. A. McDevitte and W. S. Bohn, 1869

text: That as much as he admired the greatness of their courage, since neither the fortifications of the camp, nor the height of the mountain, nor the wall of the town could retard them; in the same degree he censured their licentiousness and arrogance, because they thought that they knew more than their general concerning victory, and the issue of actions: and that he required in his soldiers forbearance and self-command, not less than valour and magnanimity.
author: Julius Caesar
speaker: Caesar
reference: Commentaries on the Gallic and Civil Wars
translation: W. A. McDevitte and W. S. Bohn, 1869

text: For neither ought the obedient to suspect that they are distrusted, nor the insolent to know that we fear them; because our fears augment the licentiousness of the latter, and diminish the zeal of the former.
author: Julius Caesar
speaker: Curio
reference: Commentaries on the Gallic and Civil Wars
locator: Civil War, Book II, Chapter XXXI
translation: W. A. McDevitte and W. S. Bohn, 1869

text: It is an honour much more brilliant than a triumph for the senate to declare its opinion, that a province has been retained rather by the uprightness and mildness of its governor, than by the strength of an army or the favour of heaven.
author: Marcus Porcius Cato the Younger
locator: Letter XX, M. Porcius Cato to Cicero

text: For certainly praise is sweet that comes from those who themselves have lived in high repute.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
locator: Letter XXI, to M. Porcius Cato

text: In all ages it has been rarer to find men capable of conquering their own desires than capable of conquering an enemy's army.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
locator: Letter XVIII, to M. Porcius Cato

text: It only remains to beg and entreat you not to set sail rashly, seamen are wont to hurry things for their own profit: be cautious, my dear Tiro: you have a wide and difficult sea before you.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero

text: With a weak army, my strongest support against the threat of a very formidable war has been my equity and purity of conduct. With these as my aids I accomplished what I never could have accomplished by any amount of legions.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
locator: Letter XVIII, to M. Porcius Cato

text: Philosophy, the best friend I have ever had in all my life, the greatest gift which has been bestowed by the gods upon mankind.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
locator: Letter XVIII, to M. Porcius Cato

text: I only employ one proof to convince me that I am loved from the heart and in sincerity, namely, that my fortune and theirs is of such a kind as to preclude any motive on their part for pretending.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
locator: Letter XXIII, to L. Papirius Paetus

text: Once depart from law, everything is uncertain; and that nothing can be guaranteed as to the future which depends on another man's will, not to say caprice.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
locator: Letter XXIII, to L. Papirius Paetus

text: I was doubly charmed by your letter, first because it made me laugh myself, and secondly because I saw that you could still laugh.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
locator: Letter XXV, to L. Papirius Paetus

text: Even that loss is less annoying when it comes from a friend than from a debtor.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
locator: Letter XXIII, to L. Papirius Paetus

text: Though genuine love is not easily distinguished from feigned, unless some crisis occurs of a kind to test faithful affection by its danger, as gold in the fire, there are other indications of a general nature.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
locator: Letter XXIII, to L. Papirius Paetus

text: If, in view of the uncertainty attaching to all wars, you had taken into consideration the possibility of our being beaten, you ought not, while fully prepared to face success, to be yet utterly unable to endure failure.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero

text: For the recollection of what I may call a common law and of the conditions of human existence softens grief.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero

text: Do we mannikins feel rebellious if one of us perishes or is killed, we whose life ought to be still shorter, when the corpses of so many towns lie in helpless ruin?
author: Servius Sulpicius Rufus
locator: Letter XXVII, Servius Sulpicius to Cicero

text: There is no sorrow beyond the power of time at length to diminish and soften.
author: Servius Sulpicius Rufus
locator: Letter XXVII, Servius Sulpicius to Cicero

text: That kind of consolation involves much distress and pain, because the relations and friends, whose part it is to offer it, are themselves overcome by an equal sorrow. They cannot attempt it without many tears, so that they seem to require consolation themselves rather than to be able to afford it to others.
author: Servius Sulpicius Rufus
locator: Letter XXVII, Servius Sulpicius to Cicero

text: In fine, do not forget that you are Cicero, and a man accustomed to instruct and advise others; and do not imitate bad physicians, who in the diseases of others profess to understand the art of healing, but are unable to prescribe for themselves.
author: Servius Sulpicius Rufus
locator: Letter XXVII, Servius Sulpicius to Cicero

text: We have seen you on many occasions bear good fortune with a noble dignity... now is the time for you to convince us that you are able to bear bad fortune equally well.
author: Servius Sulpicius Rufus
locator: Letter XXVII, Servius Sulpicius to Cicero

text: It will be said, after all it is an evil to lose one's children. Yes, it is: only it is a worse one to endure and submit to the present state of things.
author: Servius Sulpicius Rufus
locator: Letter XXVII, Servius Sulpicius to Cicero

text: The first bond of union is that between husband and wife; the next, that between parents and children; then we find one home, with everything in common.
author: Cicero

text: Man not only loves himself, but seeks another whose spirit he may so blend with his own as almost to make one being of two.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: It is not then properly friendship at all when the one will not listen to the truth, and the other is prepared to lie.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: They are not at all vexed at having committed a fault, but very angry at being reproved for it. On the contrary, they ought to be grieved at the crime and glad of the correction.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: As we are not beneficent and liberal with any view of extorting gratitude, and do not regard an act of kindness as an investment, but follow a natural inclination to liberality; so we look on friendship as worth trying for, not because we are attracted to it by the expectation of ulterior gain, but in the conviction that what it has to give us is from first to last included in the feeling itself.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Let there be only a proper husbanding of strength, and let each man proportion his efforts to his powers.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Cato
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: There is no business and no course of action demanded from us by our honour which you can consistently decline, or lay aside when begun, from a mere wish to escape from anxiety. Nay, if we wish to avoid anxiety we must avoid virtue itself.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Tarquin observed in his exile that he never knew which of his friends were real and which sham, until he had ceased to be able to repay either.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Even if those possessions, which are, in a manner, the gifts of fortune, do prove permanent, life can never be anything but joyless which is without the consolations and companionship of friends.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: For the essence of friendship being that two minds become as one, how can that ever take place if the mind of each of the separate parties to it is not single and uniform, but variable, changeable, and complex?
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: If it were true that its material advantages cemented friendship, it would be equally true that any change in them would dissolve it. But nature being incapable of change, it follows that genuine friendships are eternal.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Now the harvest of old age is, as I have often said, the memory and rich store of blessings laid up in easier life.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Cato
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Our first object, then, should be to prevent a breach; our second, to secure that, if it does occur, our friendship should seem to have died a natural rather than a violent death.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Friendship by its nature admits of no feigning, no pretence: as far as it goes it is both genuine and spontaneous.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: The clear indication of virtue, to which a mind of like character is naturally attracted, is the beginning of friendship.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Great and numerous as are the blessings of friendship, this certainly is the sovereign one, that it gives us bright hopes for the future and forbids weakness and despair. In the face of a true friend a man sees as it were a second self.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Nothing inspires love, nothing conciliates affection, like virtue. Why, in a certain sense we may be said to feel affection even for men we have never seen, owing to their honesty and virtue.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Now the qualities we ought to look out for in making our selection are firmness, stability, constancy. There is a plentiful lack of men so endowed, and it is difficult to form a judgment without testing.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: To give and receive advice, the former with freedom and yet without bitterness, the latter with patience and without irritation, is peculiarly appropriate to genuine friendship.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Indeed I am inclined to think that friends ought at times to be in want of something.... It is not friendship, then, that follows material advantage, but material advantage friendship.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: The real limit to be observed in friendship is this: the characters of two friends must be stainless. There must be complete harmony of interests, purpose, and aims, without exception.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: In friendship, let the influence of friends who give good advice be paramount; and let this influence be used to enforce advice not only in plain-spoken terms, but sometimes, if the case demands it, with sharpness; and when so used, let it be obeyed.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Bad men must have the fear of punishment before their eyes: a punishment not less severe for those who follow than for those who lead others to crime.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: This flattery, injurious as it is, can hurt no one but the man who takes it in and likes it. And it follows that the man to open his ears widest to flatterers is he who first flatters himself and is fondest of himself.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: How many things there are which we would never have done for our own sakes, but do for the sake of a friend!
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: The course of life is fixed, and nature admits of its being run but in one way, and only once; and to each part of our life there is something specially seasonable; so that the feebleness of children, as well as the high spirit of youth, the soberness of maturer years, and the ripe wisdom of old age, all have a certain natural advantage which should be secured in its proper season.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Cato
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: We must by no means abjure virtue, which secures us affection.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: True friendship appears to me to be something richer and more generous than that comes to; and not to be so narrowly on its guard against giving more than it receives.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Most people not only recognize nothing as good in our life unless it is profitable, but look upon friends as so much stock, caring most for those by whom they hope to make most profit.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Neither white hairs nor wrinkles can at once claim influence in themselves: it is the honourable conduct of earlier days that is rewarded by possessing influence at the last.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Cato
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: He used to complain that there was nothing on which men bestowed so little pains: that every one could tell exactly how many goats or sheep he had, but not how many friends.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: There are many advantages too which men of upright character voluntarily forego, or of which they are content to be deprived, that their friends may enjoy them rather than themselves.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Friendship is the one thing about the utility of which everybody with one accord is agreed.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: They are like men who would say that a steersman does nothing in sailing a ship, because, while some of the crew are climbing the masts, others hurrying up and down the gangways, others pumping out the bilge water, he sits quietly in the stern holding the tiller. He does not do what young men do; nevertheless he does what is much more important and better.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Cato
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Friendship embraces innumerable advantages. Turn which way you please, you will find it at hand. It is everywhere; and yet never out of place, never unwelcome.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: The hour of need shews the friend indeed.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Plain speaking is a cause of trouble, if the result of it is resentment, which is poison of friendship; but compliance is really the cause of much more trouble, because by indulging his faults it lets a friend plunge into headlong ruin.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: I must at the very beginning lay down this principle, friendship can only exist between good men.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: In such cases friendships should be allowed to die out gradually by an intermission of intercourse. They should, as I have been told that Cato used to say, rather be unstitched than torn in twain.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Another good rule in friendship is this: do not let an excessive affection hinder the highest interests of your friends.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Nor was I, in fact, ever wont to measure my enjoyment even of these banquets by the physical pleasures they gave more than by the gathering and conversation of friends.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Cato
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Why should we banish friendship from our lives, for fear of being involved by it in some amount of distress? If you take away emotion, what difference remains I don't say between a man and a beast, but between a man and a stone or a log of wood?
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Nor is it the body alone that must be supported, but the intellect and soul much more. For they are like lamps: unless you feed them with oil, they too go out from old age.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Cato
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: The fact is that old age is respectable just as long as it asserts itself, maintains its proper rights, and is not enslaved to any one. For as I admire a young man who has something of the old man in him, so do I an old one who has something of a young man.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Cato
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Nothing is really more delightful than a return of affection, and the mutual interchange of kind feeling and good offices.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: An open flatterer any one can detect, unless he is an absolute fool the covert insinuation of the cunning and the sly is what we have to be studiously on our guard against.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: Just as it is not every wine, so it is not every life, that turns sour from keeping. Serious gravity I approve of in old age, but, as in other things, it must be within due limits: bitterness I can in no case approve.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Cato
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: If virtue be neglected, those who imagine themselves to possess friends will find out their error as soon as some grave disaster forces them to make trial of them.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: If a man could ascend to heaven and get a clear view of the natural order of the universe, and the beauty of the heavenly bodies, that wonderful spectacle would give him small pleasure, though nothing could be conceived more delightful if he had but had some one to whom to tell what he had seen.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: For not only is Fortune blind herself; but she generally makes those blind also who enjoy her favours. They are carried, so to speak, beyond themselves with self-conceit and self-will; nor can anything be more perfectly intolerable than a successful fool.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: People who are always bringing up their services are a nuisance. The recipient ought to remember them; the performer should never mention them.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: One thing leads to another; and once set going, the downward course proceeds with ever-increasing velocity.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: There are people who owe more to bitter enemies than to apparently pleasant friends: the former often speak the truth, the latter never.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: If we remonstrate, it should be without bitterness; if we reprove, there should be no word of insult.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: The intercourse between friends is varied and complex, and it must often happen that causes of suspicion and offence arise, which a wise man will sometimes avoid, at other times remove, at others treat with indulgence.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: For the advantages of genius and virtue, and in short, of every kind of superiority, are never realized to their fullest extent until they are bestowed upon our nearest and dearest.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: No such confederation of evilly disposed men must be allowed to shelter itself under the plea of friendship, but that, on the contrary, it must be visited with the severest punishment, lest the idea should prevail that fidelity to a friend justifies even making war upon one's country.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: This sort of man is rare; and indeed all excellent things are rare; and nothing in the world is so hard to find as a thing entirely and completely perfect of its kind.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: If we are prudent then, we shall rein in our impulse to affection as we do chariot horses. We make a preliminary trial of horses. So we should of friendship; and should test our friends' characters by a kind of tentative friendship.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: It is not so much what one gets by a friend that gives one pleasure, as the warmth of his feeling; and we only care for a friend's service if it has been prompted by affection.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: What can be more foolish than to regard the uncertain as certain, the false as true?
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Cato
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: I conclude, then, that the plea of having acted in the interests of a friend is not a valid excuse for a wrong action. For, seeing that a belief in a man's virtue is the original cause of friendship, friendship can hardly remain if virtue he abandoned.
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
speaker: Laelius
reference: Treatises on Friendship and Old Age
location: Rome or his villa at Tusculum, Italy (presumed)

text: It often happens that a man has too humble an idea of himself, or takes too despairing a view of his chance of bettering his fortune.
