text: It is a moste difficult thyng, an armie beyng now moved to flie, to staie it, and make it to faight.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: A Capitayne oughte amonge all other of his affaires, with al subtiltie to devise to devide the force of the enemie, either with makyng him to suspecte his owne menne, in whome he trusteth, or to give him occasion, that he maye seperate his menne, and therby to be come more weake.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: The good orders, without the souldiours help, no lesse or otherwise doe disorder, then the habitacion of a sumptuous and roiall palais, although it wer decte with gold and precious stones, when without being covered, should not have wherewith to defende it from the raine.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli

text: The number of L. M. souldiers ought not to bee passed, but rather to take lesse: because manie make confucion, nor suffer not the discipline to be observed, and the orders learned.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: It was the duty of a good general to be the first man in the saddle and the last out of it.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
locator: The Life of Castruccio Castracani of Lucca
location: Sant'Andrea in Percussina, near Florence, Italy

text: It is lesse errour to take them al, to arme theim and exercise theim, beyng not able to knowe, whiche of theim is beste, and to reserve to make after more certaine chosen, when in practisyng theim with exercise, there shall be knowen those of moste spirite, and of moste life.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: Never conducte thy men to faight the field, if first them hast not confirmed their mindes and knowest them to be without feare, and to be in good order: for thou oughteste never to enterprise any dangerous thyng with thy souldiours, but when thou seest, that they hope to overcome.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: A wall, whiche on every parte enclineth, requireth rather to have many proppes, and thicke, although not so strong, then fewe, though thei were strong: bicause the vertue of one a lone, doeth not remedie the ruine a farre of.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: When men marche thoroughe the enemies countrey, they ar in muche more, and greater perils, then in fayghtyng the fielde.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: The sodene accidentes, with difficultie are reamedied: those that are thought upon, with facilitie.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: That prince, or common weale, whiche should appoincte to make a newe power, and cause reputacion to their armie, ought to accustome the Souldiours thereof, to heare the capitain to speake, and the capitain to know how to speake unto them.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: In marchyng, advertismente ought to be had, that the one parte of the armie goe not a sunder from the other, or that thoroughe some goyng fast, and some softe, the armie become not slender: the whiche thynges, be occation of dissorder: therfore the heddes muste be placed in suche wise, that they may maintaine the pace even, causing to goe softe those that goe to fast, and to haste forward the other that goe to sloe.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: The knowlege to faight, maketh men more bold, bicause no man feareth to doe that thing, which he thinketh to have learned to dooe.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: Men out of order, have feare of those that be in araie.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: He who is considered wise by day will not be considered a fool at night.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Castruccio Castracani
locator: The Life of Castruccio Castracani of Lucca
location: Sant'Andrea in Percussina, near Florence, Italy

text: Obstinatenesse is increased by the confidence, and love of the Capitaine, or of the countrie. Confidence is caused through the armour, the order the late victorie, and the opinion of the Capitaine. The love of the countrie, is caused of nature: that of the Capitain, through vertue, more then by any other benefite.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: An armie is not made coragious, bicause in thesame be hardie menne, but by reason the orders thereof bee well appoineted: For as moche as if I be one of the first faighters, and do knowe, beyng overcome, where I maie retire, and who hath to succeade in my place, I shall alwaies faight with boldnes, seing my succour at hand.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: That, which above all other thynge kepeth the armie in unitee, is the reputacion of the Capitaine, the whiche onely groweth of his vertue: because neither bloud, nor authoritie gave it ever without vertue.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: The souldiour becometh more covetous to spoyle, and lesse observeth the orders: and manie times it hath been seen, howe the covetousnesse of the praye, hath made those to leese, whome were victorious.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: Princes, especially those that are new, have found more faith and profit in those men, who in the beginning of their State, have been held suspected, than in those who at their entrance have been their confidents.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli

text: Discipline maie doe more in warre, then furie.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: It is meete, that the Capitaine be moste experte, in the knowlege of situacions of countries, and have aboute him divers men, that have the verie same expertenes.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: A king ought not to desire to have about him, any that is not of this condicion if he be wise, and prudently minde to governe: for that, that if he shal have about him either to muche lovers of peace, or to much lovers of warre, they shall make him to erre.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: In the faight never occupie a battell to any other thyng, then to the same, for whiche thou haste apoineted it, if thou wilt make no disorder.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: A Prince ought to ordaine his armie, as expedite as is possible, and take from thesame all those thynges, whiche maie cause any trouble or burthen unto it, and make unto hym any enterprise difficulte.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: The greateste parte of prudent capitaines, rather receive the violence of the enemies, then go with violence to assalte them: for that the furie is easely withstoode of sure and steddie menne, and the furie beyng sustained, converteth lightly into vilenesse.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: The errours that I maie happen to make by writing, may be without harme to any man corrected: but those the whiche of them be made in doyng cannot be knowen without the ruine of Empires.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli

text: To know in the warre how to understande occasion, and to take it, helpeth more then anie other thynge.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: It importeth more then any thyng, to have the souldiours to know how to set themselves in araie quickly... for asmoche as the souldiours, whiche can doe this well, be expert souldiours, and although thei have never seen enemies in the face, thei maie be called old souldiours, and contrariwise, those whiche cannot keepe these orders, though thei have been in a thousande warres, thei ought alwaies to be reputed new souldiours.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: He that can wel order a fielde against the enemie, the other faultes that he should make in the affaires of warre, wilbe borne with: but he that lacketh this knowledge, although that in other particulars he be verie good, he shal never bring a warre to honor.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: I would not care, that there were sixe men of like degree, to thintent, that every one of them might strive, who should doe beste.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: The besieged ought to use more diligence in the warde, when the enemie is gone from theim, then when he is at hande.
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
speaker: Fabrizio Colonna

text: I condemn all violence in the education of a tender soul that is designed for honour and liberty. There is I know not what of servile in rigour and constraint; and I am of opinion that what is not to be done by reason, prudence, and address, is never to be affected by force.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book II, Chapter 8, Of the Affection of Fathers to their Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: Obedience is never pure nor calm in him who reasons and disputes.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book II, Chapter XVII, Of Presumption
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: The father and the son may be of quite contrary humours, and so of brothers: he is my son, he is my brother; but he is passionate, ill-natured, or a fool.
author: Michel de Montaigne
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: It is not enough to fortify his soul; you are also to make his sinews strong; for the soul will be oppressed if not assisted by the members, and would have too hard a task to discharge two offices alone.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, Chapter 25, Of the Education of Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: The confidence in another man's virtue is no light evidence of a man's own, and God willingly favours such a confidence.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, Chapter XL, That the Relish for Good and Evil Depends upon the Opinion We Have of Them
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: Let him be able to do everything, but love to do nothing but what is good.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, Chapter 25, Of the Education of Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: There is nothing to which nature seems so much to have inclined us, as to society; and Aristotle, says that the good legislators had more respect to friendship than to justice.
author: Michel de Montaigne
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: I see no marriages where the conjugal compatibility sooner fails than those that we contract upon the account of beauty and amorous desires; there should be more solid and constant foundation, and they should proceed with greater circumspection; this furious ardour is worth nothing.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book III, Chapter V, Upon Some Verses of Virgil
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: Friendship, on the contrary, is enjoyed proportionably as it is desired; and only grows up, is nourished and improved by enjoyment, as being of itself spiritual, and the soul growing still more refined by practice.
author: Michel de Montaigne
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: Make him understand, that to acknowledge the error he shall discover in his own argument, though only found out by himself, is an effect of judgment and sincerity... that obstinacy and contention are common qualities, most appearing in mean souls; that to revise and correct himself, to forsake an unjust argument in the height and heat of dispute, are rare, great, and philosophical qualities.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, Chapter 25, Of the Education of Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: A father worn out with age and infirmities, and deprived by weakness and want of health of the common society of men, wrongs himself and his to amass a great heap of treasure.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book II, Chapter 8, Of the Affection of Fathers to their Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: For neither are all the secret thoughts of fathers fit to be communicated to children, lest it beget an indecent familiarity betwixt them; nor can the advices and reproofs, which is one of the principal offices of friendship, be properly performed by the son to the father.
author: Michel de Montaigne
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: For though one may almost everywhere meet with men sufficiently qualified for a superficial acquaintance, yet in this, where a man is to deal from the very bottom of his heart, without any manner of reservation, it will be requisite that all the wards and springs be truly wrought and perfectly sure.
author: Michel de Montaigne
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: Men do not marry for themselves, let them say what they will; they marry as much or more for their posterity and family; the custom and interest of marriage concern our race much more than us.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book III, Chapter V, Upon Some Verses of Virgil
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: Permitting his pupil himself to taste things, and of himself to discern and choose them, sometimes opening the way to him, and sometimes leaving him to open it for himself; that is, I would not have him alone to invent and speak, but that he should also hear his pupil speak in turn.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, Chapter 25, Of the Education of Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: A true and regular affection ought to spring and increase with the knowledge they give us of themselves, and then, if they are worthy of it, the natural propension walking hand in hand with reason, to cherish them with a truly paternal love.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book II, Chapter 8, Of the Affection of Fathers to their Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: By how much these are friendships that the law and natural obligation impose upon us, so much less is there of our own choice and voluntary freedom; whereas that voluntary liberty of ours has no production more promptly and properly its own than affection and friendship.
author: Michel de Montaigne
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: In the friendship I speak of, they mix and work themselves into one piece, with so universal a mixture, that there is no more sign of the seam by which they were first conjoined. If a man should importune me to give a reason why I loved him, I find it could no otherwise be expressed, than by making answer: because it was he, because it was I.
author: Michel de Montaigne
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: I would endeavour by pleasant conversation to create in my children a warm and unfeigned friendship and good-will towards me, which in well-descended natures is not hard to do.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book II, Chapter 8, Of the Affection of Fathers to their Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: Common friendships will admit of division; one may love the beauty of this person, the good-humour of that, the liberality of a third, the paternal affection of a fourth, the fraternal love of a fifth, and so of the rest: but this friendship that possesses the whole soul, and there rules and sways with an absolute sovereignty, cannot possibly admit of a rival.
author: Michel de Montaigne
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: As concerning marriage, besides that it is a covenant, the entrance into which only is free, but the continuance in it forced and compulsory, having another dependence than that of our own free will, and a bargain commonly contracted to other ends, there almost always happens a thousand intricacies in it to unravel, enough to break the thread and to divert the current of a lively affection: whereas friendship has no manner of business or traffic with aught but itself.
author: Michel de Montaigne
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: Instead of gathering observations from others, we make it our whole business to lay ourselves open to them, and are more concerned how to expose and set out our own commodities, than how to increase our stock by acquiring new. Silence, therefore, and modesty are very advantageous qualities in conversation.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, Chapter 25, Of the Education of Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: I have only led a languishing life; and the very pleasures that present themselves to me, instead of administering anything of consolation, double my affliction for his loss. We were halves throughout, and to that degree, that methinks, by outliving him, I defraud him of his part.
author: Michel de Montaigne
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: They begin to teach us to live when we have almost done living.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, Chapter 25, Of the Education of Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: The greatest and most important difficulty of human science is the education of children.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, Chapter 25, Of the Education of Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: Now in this initiation of our studies in their progress, whatsoever presents itself before us is book sufficient; a roguish trick of a page, a sottish mistake of a servant, a jest at the table, are so many new subjects.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, Chapter 25, Of the Education of Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: As to the rest, this method of education ought to be carried on with a severe sweetness, quite contrary to the practice of our pedants, who, instead of tempting and alluring children to letters by apt and gentle ways, do in truth present nothing before them but rods and ferules, horror and cruelty.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, Chapter 25, Of the Education of Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: Human understanding is marvellously enlightened by daily conversation with men, for we are, otherwise, compressed and heaped up in ourselves, and have our sight limited to the length of our own noses.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, Chapter 25, Of the Education of Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: Love him... so as if you were one day to hate him; and hate him so as you were one day to love him.
author: Michel de Montaigne
speaker: Chilo
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: To know by rote, is no knowledge, and signifies no more but only to retain what one has intrusted to our memory. That which a man rightly knows and understands, he is the free disposer of at his own full liberty, without any regard to the author from whence he had it, or fumbling over the leaves of his book.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, Chapter 25, Of the Education of Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: Such as have lean and spare bodies stuff themselves out with clothes; so they who are defective in matter endeavour to make amends with words.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, Chapter 25, Of the Education of Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: Mothers are too tender, and their natural affection is apt to make the most discreet of them all so overfond, that they can neither find in their hearts to give them due correction for the faults they may commit, nor suffer them to be inured to hardships and hazards, as they ought to be.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, Chapter 25, Of the Education of Children
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: Ordinary inconveniences are never light; they are continual and inseparable, especially when they spring from the members of a family, continual and inseparable.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book III, Chapter IX, Of Vanity
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: Those who preach to princes so circumspect and vigilant a jealousy and distrust, under colour of security, preach to them ruin and dishonour: nothing noble can be performed without danger.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, Chapter XXIII, Various Events from the Same Counsel
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: In those other ordinary friendships, you are to walk with bridle in your hand, with prudence and circumspection, for in them the knot is not so sure that a man may not half suspect it will slip.
author: Michel de Montaigne
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

text: It is a very unbecoming rudeness to carp at everything that is not agreeable to our own palate. Let him be satisfied with correcting himself, and not seem to condemn everything in another he would not do himself.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, Chapter 25, Of the Education of Children

reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We distrust the sincerity of those whom we talk with, we always believe them more sincere with us than with others.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We have all sufficient strength to support the misfortunes of others.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We may forgive those who bore us, we cannot forgive those whom we bore.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: What men term friendship is merely a partnership with a collection of reciprocal interests, and an exchange of favours.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: What we call liberality is often but the vanity of giving, which we like more than that we give away.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Sovereign ability consists in knowing the value of things.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Those who apply themselves too closely to little things often become incapable of great things.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Those who lay down rules too often break them, and the safest we are able to give is to listen much, to speak little, and to say nothing that will ever give ground for regret.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: A man is perhaps ungrateful, but often less chargeable with ingratitude than his benefactor is.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Nothing flatters our pride so much as the confidence of the great, because we regard it as the result of our worth, without remembering that generally 'tis but vanity, or the inability to keep a secret.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Most people judge men only by success or by fortune.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Although men flatter themselves with their great actions, they are not so often the result of a great design as of chance.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Under the pretext of weeping for one dear to us we bemoan ourselves; we regret her good opinion of us, we deplore the loss of our comfort, our pleasure, our consideration. Thus the dead have the credit of tears shed for the living.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We easily forgive in our friends those faults we do not perceive.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: A clever man ought to so regulate his interests that each will fall in due order. Our greediness so often troubles us, making us run after so many things at the same time, that while we too eagerly look after the least we miss the greatest.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: When one loves one doubts even what one most believes.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It is far safer and more honest to tell nothing than to be silent when we have begun to tell.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Yet it is necessary to listen to those who talk, we should give them the time they want, and let them say even senseless things; never contradict or interrupt them; on the contrary, we should enter into their mind and taste, illustrate their meaning, praise anything they say that deserves praise.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It is not so dangerous to do wrong to most men, as to do them too much good.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The desire to appear clever often prevents our being so.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: A little wit with good sense bores less in the long run than much wit with ill nature.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: A well-trained mind has less difficulty in submitting to than in guiding an ill-trained mind.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We sometimes complain of the levity of our friends to justify our own by anticipation.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It is much easier to seem fitted for posts we do not fill than for those we do.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We are easily consoled at the misfortunes of our friends when they enable us to prove our tenderness for them.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The greatest skill of the least skilful is to know how to submit to the direction of another.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Renewed friendships require more care than those that have never been broken.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We hardly find any persons of good sense, save those who agree with us.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The desire which urges us to deserve praise strengthens our good qualities, and praise given to wit, valour, and beauty, tends to increase them.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Those only are despicable who fear to be despised.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: There should be some variety in wit. Those who have only one kind of wit cannot please for long unless they can take different roads, and not both use the same talents, thus adding to the pleasure of society, and keeping the same harmony that different voices and different instruments should observe in music.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We should earnestly desire but few things if we clearly knew what we desired.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Ordinary men commonly condemn what is beyond them.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We are inconsolable at being deceived by our enemies and betrayed by our friends, yet still we are often content to be thus served by ourselves.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The good we have received from a man should make us excuse the wrong he does us.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Silence is the best resolve for him who distrusts himself.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: There may be talent without position, but there is no position without some kind of talent.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Our envy always lasts longer than the happiness of those we envy.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It is far easier to know men than to know man.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Cunning and treachery are the offspring of incapacity.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The refusal of praise is only the wish to be praised twice.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Timidity is a fault which is dangerous to blame in those we desire to cure of it.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: There is no disguise which can long hide love where it exists, nor feign it where it does not.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Flattery is base coin to which only our vanity gives currency.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Rare true love is, true friendship is rarer.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: There is no praise we have not lavished upon Prudence; and yet she cannot assure to us the most trifling event.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We promise according to our hopes; we perform according to our fears.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We pardon in the degree that we love.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Young men entering life should be either shy or bold; a solemn and sedate manner usually degenerates into impertinence.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: There is no passion wherein self-love reigns so powerfully as in love, and one is always more ready to sacrifice the peace of the loved one than his own.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Pity is often a reflection of our own evils in the ills of others. It is a delicate foresight of the troubles into which we may fall. We help others that on like occasions we may be helped ourselves.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The passions are the only advocates which always persuade. They are a natural art, the rules of which are infallible; and the simplest man with passion will be more persuasive than the most eloquent without.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We become so accustomed to disguise ourselves to others that at last we are disguised to ourselves.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The heat of youth is not more opposed to safety than the coldness of age.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: 'Tis a small misfortune to oblige an ungrateful man; but it is unbearable to be obliged by a scoundrel.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Avarice often produces opposite results: there are an infinite number of persons who sacrifice their property to doubtful and distant expectations, others mistake great future advantages for small present interests.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The evil that we do does not attract to us so much persecution and hatred as our good qualities.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Nothing is so infectious as example, and we never do great good or evil without producing the like. We imitate good actions by emulation, and bad ones by the evil of our nature, which shame imprisons until example liberates.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We should make our pleasure that of other persons, to humour, never to wound their self-love.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Great and striking actions which dazzle the eyes are represented by politicians as the effect of great designs, instead of which they are commonly caused by the temper and the passions.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Usually we are more satirical from vanity than malice.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We often boast that we are never bored, but yet we are so conceited that we do not perceive how often we bore others.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: There is real love just as there are real ghosts; every person speaks of it, few persons have seen it.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We should readily excuse our friends when their faults are born with them, and they are less than their good qualities... We should try to make them perceive their faults, so as to give them the merit of correcting them.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Men will freely expose themselves at the beginning of an action, and relax and be easily discouraged if it should last.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: There are few people who would not be ashamed of being beloved when they love no longer.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Above all things we should avoid often talking of ourselves and giving ourselves as an example; nothing is more tiresome than a man who quotes himself for everything.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The gratitude of most men is but a secret desire of receiving greater benefits.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Great names degrade instead of elevating those who know not how to sustain them.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Ability wins us the esteem of the true men, luck that of the people.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: What makes the vanity of others unsupportable is that it wounds our own.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: One of the reasons that we find so few persons rational and agreeable in conversation is there is hardly a person who does not think more of what he wants to say than of his answer to what is said.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: There are men of whom we can never believe evil without having seen it. Yet there are very few in whom we should be surprised to see it.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Moderation is made a virtue to limit the ambition of the great; to console ordinary people for their small fortune and equally small ability.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Self-love is the greatest of flatterers.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It is far easier to be wise for others than to be so for oneself.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: There is a kind of greatness which does not depend upon fortune: it is a certain manner what distinguishes us, and which seems to destine us for great things; it is the value we insensibly set upon ourselves; it is by this quality that we gain the deference of other men.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: When fortune surprises us by giving us some great office without having gradually led us to expect it, or without having raised our hopes, it is well nigh impossible to occupy it well, and to appear worthy to fill it.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: He is a truly good man who desires always to bear the inspection of good men.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It is not wrong to retain our opinions if they are reasonable, but we should yield to reason, wherever she appears and from whatever side she comes, she alone should govern our opinions.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The test of extraordinary merit is to see those who envy it the most yet obliged to praise it.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: If there is a pure love, exempt from the mixture of our other passions, it is that which is concealed at the bottom of the heart and of which even ourselves are ignorant.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: When our hatred is too bitter it places us below those whom we hate.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: In great matters we should not try so much to create opportunities as to utilise those that offer themselves.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It is dangerous to seek to be always the leader of the conversation, and to push a good argument too hard, when we have found one. Civility often hides half its understanding, and when it meets with an opinionated man who defends the bad side, spares him the disgrace of giving way.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Envy is destroyed by true friendship, flirtation by true love.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Usually we only praise to be praised.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It is more necessary to study men than books.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The reason why so few persons are agreeable in conversation is that each thinks more of what he desires to say, than of what the others say, and that we make bad listeners when we want to speak.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: If we never flattered ourselves the flattery of others would not hurt us.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: If we judge of love by the majority of its results it rather resembles hatred than friendship.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It is far better to accustom our mind to bear the ills we have than to speculate on those which may befall us.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The daily employment of cunning marks a little mind, it generally happens that those who resort to it in one respect to protect themselves lay themselves open to attack in another.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: He who thinks he has the power to content the world greatly deceives himself, but he who thinks that the world cannot be content with him deceives himself yet more.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It is a proof of little friendship not to perceive the growing coolness of that of our friends.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It is impossible to love a second time those whom we have really ceased to love.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We should often be ashamed of our very best actions if the world only saw the motives which caused them.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Jealousy is the worst of all evils, yet the one that is least pitied by those who cause it.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The wise man finds it better not to enter the encounter than to conquer.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Some reproaches praise; some praises reproach.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The confidence we have in ourselves arises in a great measure from that that we have in others.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: In love deceit almost always goes further than mistrust.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We do not regret the loss of our friends according to their merits, but according to OUR wants, and the opinion with which we believed we had impressed them of our worth.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Almost all the world takes pleasure in paying small debts; many people show gratitude for trifling, but there is hardly one who does not show ingratitude for great favours.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The most subtle of our acts is to simulate blindness for snares that we know are set for us. We are never so easily deceived as when trying to deceive.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: What makes false reckoning, as regards gratitude, is that the pride of the giver and the receiver cannot agree as to the value of the benefit.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Absence extinguishes small passions and increases great ones, as the wind will blow out a candle, and blow in a fire.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Vices enter into the composition of virtues as poison into that of medicines. Prudence collects and blends the two and renders them useful against the ills of life.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We have more strength than will; and it is often merely for an excuse we say things are impossible.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It is generally the fault of the loved one not to perceive when love ceases.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: There is great ability in knowing how to conceal one's ability.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Why we hate with so much bitterness those who deceive us is because they think themselves more clever than we are.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Self love increases or diminishes for us the good qualities of our friends, in proportion to the satisfaction we feel with them, and we judge of their merit by the manner in which they act towards us.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: There are no accidents so unfortunate from which skilful men will not draw some advantage, nor so fortunate that foolish men will not turn them to their hurt.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Everyone seeks to find his pleasure and his advantage at the expense of others. We prefer ourselves always to those with whom we intend to live, and they almost always perceive the preference. It is this which disturbs and destroys society.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It is difficult to love those we do not esteem, but it is no less so to love those whom we esteem much more than ourselves.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We always like those who admire us, we do not always like those whom we admire.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Most young people think they are natural when they are only boorish and rude.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It is easier to govern others than to prevent being governed.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The art of using moderate abilities to advantage wins praise, and often acquires more reputation than real brilliancy.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We may seem great in a post beneath our capacity, but we oftener seem little in a post above it.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The extreme delight we take in talking of ourselves should warn us that it is not shared by those who listen.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It is only people who possess firmness who can possess true gentleness. In those who appear gentle it is generally only weakness, which is readily converted into harshness.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: A man to whom no one is pleasing is much more unhappy than one who pleases nobody.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: If we take the liberty to dwell on their faults we cannot long preserve the feelings we should hold towards our friends and benefactors.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The greatest effort of friendship is not to show our faults to a friend, but to show him his own.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The most certain sign of being born with great qualities is to be born without envy.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: As in friendship so in love, we are often happier from ignorance than from knowledge.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Constancy in love is a perpetual inconstancy which causes our heart to attach itself to all the qualities of the person we love in succession, sometimes giving the preference to one, sometimes to another.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Little minds are too much wounded by little things; great minds see all and are not even hurt.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Magnanimity despises all, to win all.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Whatever great advantages nature may give, it is not she alone, but fortune also that makes the hero.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: There is no less eloquence in the voice, in the eyes and in the air of a speaker than in his choice of words.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Jealousy is always born with love, but does not always die with it.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Men are not only prone to forget benefits and injuries; they even hate those who have obliged them, and cease to hate those who have injured them. The necessity of revenging an injury or of recompensing a benefit seems a slavery to which they are unwilling to submit.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Moderation is caused by the fear of exciting the envy and contempt which those merit who are intoxicated with their good fortune; it is a vain display of our strength of mind, and in short the moderation of men at their greatest height is only a desire to appear greater than their fortune.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Falsely honest men are those who disguise their faults both to themselves and others; truly honest men are those who know them perfectly and confess them.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: For us to be always good, others should believe that they cannot behave wickedly to us with impunity.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Intrepidity is an extraordinary strength of soul which raises it above the troubles, disorders, and emotions which the sight of great perils can arouse in it: by this strength heroes maintain a calm aspect and preserve their reason and liberty in the most surprising and terrible accidents.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: One honour won is a surety for more.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Envy is more irreconcilable than hatred.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: What renders us so changeable in our friendship is, that it is difficult to know the qualities of the soul, but easy to know those of the mind.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Youth is a continual intoxication; it is the fever of reason.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We should anticipate what can please our friends, find out how to be useful to them so as to exempt them from annoyance, and when we cannot avert evils, seem to participate in them.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Fortune makes visible our virtues or our vices, as light does objects.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Sincerity is an openness of heart; we find it in very few people; what we usually see is only an artful dissimulation to win the confidence of others.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Nothing is less sincere than the way of asking and giving advice. The person asking seems to pay deference to the opinion of his friend, while thinking in reality of making his friend approve his opinion and be responsible for his conduct.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: A quickness in believing evil without having sufficiently examined it, is the effect of pride and laziness. We wish to find the guilty, and we do not wish to trouble ourselves in examining the crime.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Pride has a larger part than goodness in our remonstrances with those who commit faults, and we reprove them not so much to correct as to persuade them that we ourselves are free from faults.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Reconciliation with our enemies is but a desire to better our condition, a weariness of war, the fear of some unlucky accident.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Men would not live long in society were they not the dupes of each other.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We need greater virtues to sustain good than evil fortune.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Perfect valour is to do without witnesses what one would do before all the world.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: A man cannot please long who has only one kind of wit.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We are more humiliated by the least infidelity towards us, than by our greatest towards others.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: In the intercourse of life, we please more by our faults than by our good qualities.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We should gain more by letting the world see what we are than by trying to seem what we are not.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We well know that it is bad taste to talk of our wives; but we do not so well know that it is the same to speak of ourselves.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: There are matters and maladies which at certain times remedies only serve to make worse; true skill consists in knowing when it is dangerous to use them.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: As it is the mark of great minds to say many things in a few words, so it is that of little minds to use many words to say nothing.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Our enemies come nearer the truth in the opinions they form of us than we do in our opinion of ourselves.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: No people are more often wrong than those who will not allow themselves to be wrong.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We should manage fortune like our health, enjoy it when it is good, be patient when it is bad, and never resort to strong remedies but in an extremity.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: To praise good actions heartily is in some measure to take part in them.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We often persuade ourselves to love people who are more powerful than we are, yet interest alone produces our friendship; we do not give our hearts away for the good we wish to do, but for that we expect to receive.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Interest speaks all sorts of tongues and plays all sorts of characters; even that of disinterestedness.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: True eloquence consists in saying all that should be, not all that could be said.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We would rather see those to whom we have done a benefit, than those who have done us one.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Neither love nor fire can subsist without perpetual motion; both cease to live so soon as they cease to hope, or to fear.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Self love is more cunning than the most cunning man in the world.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Sometimes there is not less ability in knowing how to use than in giving good advice.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We should not judge of a man's merit by his great abilities, but by the use he makes of them.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: If there is much art in speaking to the purpose, there is no less in knowing when to be silent. There is an eloquent silence which serves to approve or to condemn, there is a silence of discretion and of respect.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Nature makes merit but fortune sets it to work.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We have not the courage to say generally that we have no faults, and that our enemies have no good qualities; but in fact we are not far from believing so.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: If we had no faults we should not take so much pleasure in noting those of others.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The intention of never deceiving often exposes us to deception.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The desire of talking about ourselves, and of putting our faults in the light we wish them to be seen, forms a great part of our sincerity.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The charm of novelty and old custom, however opposite to each other, equally blind us to the faults of our friends.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Complaisance is essential in society, but it should have its limits, it becomes a slavery when it is extreme. We should so render a free consent, that in following the opinion of our friends they should believe that they follow ours.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Weak persons cannot be sincere.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: A man often believes himself leader when he is led; as his mind endeavours to reach one goal, his heart insensibly drags him towards another.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We are nearer loving those who hate us, than those who love us more than we desire.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: When we love too much it is difficult to discover when we have ceased to be beloved.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We find very few ungrateful people when we are able to confer favours.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Few are sufficiently wise to prefer censure which is useful to praise which is treacherous.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Idleness, languishing as she is, does not often fail in being mistress; she usurps authority over all the plans and actions of life; imperceptibly consuming and destroying both passions and virtues.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Luxury and too refined a policy in states are a sure presage of their fall, because all parties looking after their own interest turn away from the public good.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Most men, like plants, possess hidden qualities which chance discovers.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: A true friend is the greatest of all goods, and that of which we think least of acquiring.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Confidence always pleases those who receive it. It is a tribute we pay to their merit, a deposit we commit to their trust, a pledge which gives them a claim upon us, a kind of dependence to which we voluntarily submit.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Quarrels would not last long if the fault was only on one side.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Nothing is rarer than true good nature, those who think they have it are generally only pliant or weak.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Civility is but a desire to receive civility, and to be esteemed polite.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It is not enough to have great qualities, we should also have the management of them.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Jealousy lives upon doubt; and comes to an end or becomes a fury as soon as it passes from doubt to certainty.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: There are none who press so heavily on others as the lazy ones, when they have satisfied their idleness, and wish to appear industrious.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: A man is often more clever than one other, but not than all others.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Gratitude is as the good faith of merchants: it holds commerce together; and we do not pay because it is just to pay debts, but because we shall thereby more easily find people who will lend.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Prudence and love are not made for each other; in the ratio that love increases, prudence diminishes.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We may bestow advice, but we cannot inspire the conduct.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Brilliant an action it should not be esteemed great unless the result of a great motive.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Few things are impossible in themselves; application to make them succeed fails us more often than the means.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The fidelity of most men is merely an invention of self-love to win confidence; a method to place us above others and to render us depositaries of the most important matters.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Great souls are not those who have fewer passions and more virtues than the common, but those only who have greater designs.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Most friends sicken us of friendship, most devotees of devotion.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It sometimes happens that persons opposite in temper and mind become united. They doubtless hold together for different reasons, which cannot last for long.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The clemency of Princes is often but policy to win the affections of the people.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Sometimes we lose friends for whose loss our regret is greater than our grief, and others for whom our grief is greater than our regret.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The agreement we meet between minds would not keep society together for long if she was not governed and sustained by good sense, temper, and by the consideration which ought to exist between persons who have to live together.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The true way to be deceived is to think oneself more knowing than others.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: A confidence in being able to please is often an infallible means of being displeasing.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We should never say anything with an air of authority, nor show any superiority of mind. We should avoid far-fetched expressions, expressions hard or forced, and never let the words be grander than the matter.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: How shall we hope that another person will keep our secret if we do not keep it ourselves.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: To understand matters rightly we should understand their details, and as that knowledge is almost infinite, our knowledge is always superficial and imperfect.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
