reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: That man who has never been in danger cannot answer for his courage.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: It appears that nature has hid at the bottom of our hearts talents and abilities unknown to us. It is only the passions that have the power of bringing them to light.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: There is often more pride than goodness in our grief for our enemies' miseries; it is to show how superior we are to them, that we bestow on them the sign of our compassion.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Those faults are always pardonable that we have the courage to avow.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: There is more self-love than love in jealousy.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Jealousy is in a manner just and reasonable, as it tends to preserve a good which belongs, or which we believe belongs to us, on the other hand envy is a fury which cannot endure the happiness of others.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The pleasure of love is in loving, we are happier in the passion we feel than in that we inspire.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Man's merit, like the crops, has its season.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The fame of great men ought always to be estimated by the means used to acquire it.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Opportunity makes us known to others, but more to ourselves.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: We can love nothing but what agrees with us, and we can only follow our taste or our pleasure when we prefer our friends to ourselves; nevertheless it is only by that preference that friendship can be true and perfect.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Nothing is given so profusely as advice.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: The greatest mistake of penetration is not to have fallen short, but to have gone too far.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: All passions make us commit some faults, love alone makes us ridiculous.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Kings do with men as with pieces of money; they make them bear what value they will, and one is forced to receive them according to their currency value, and not at their true worth.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: Whatever disgrace we may have deserved, it is almost always in our power to re-establish our character.
author: Francois de La Rochefoucauld
reference: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell, 1871

text: If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of Giants.
author: Isaac Newton

text: If ever two were one, then surely we. If ever man were loved by wife, then thee.
author: Anne Bradstreet
reference: To My Dear and Loving Husband

text: That few in public affairs act from a mere view of the good of their country, whatever they may pretend... That fewer still, in public affairs, act with a view to the good of mankind.
author: Benjamin Franklin
locator: Chapter IX, Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection, Observations on my reading history

text: That the great affairs of the world, the wars, revolutions, etc., are carried on and effected by parties. That the view of these parties is their present general interest, or what they take to be such. That the different views of these different parties occasion all confusion.
author: Benjamin Franklin
locator: Chapter IX, Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection, Observations on my reading history

text: That while a party is carrying on a general design, each man has his particular private interest in view. That as soon as a party has gain'd its general point, each member becomes intent upon his particular interest; which, thwarting others, breaks that party into divisions, and occasions more confusion.
author: Benjamin Franklin
locator: Chapter IX, Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection, Observations on my reading history

text: There seems to me at present to be great occasion for raising a United Party for Virtue, by forming the virtuous and good men of all nations into a regular body, to be govern'd by suitable good and wise rules, which good and wise men may probably be more unanimous in their obedience to, than common people are to common laws.
author: Benjamin Franklin
locator: Chapter IX, Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection, Observations on my reading history

text: Thus God and Nature link'd the gen'ral frame, And bade Self-love and Social be the same.
author: Alexander Pope

text: If, therefore, you would rather please than offend, rather be well than ill spoken of, rather be loved than hated; remember to have that constant attention about you which flatters every man's little vanity; and the want of which, by mortifying his pride, never fails to excite his resentment, or at least his ill will.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter I, to his son, Bath, October 9, Old Style 1746

text: As your affection for me can only proceed from your experience and conviction of my fondness for you (for to talk of natural affection is talking nonsense), the only return I desire is, what it is chiefly your interest to make me; I mean your invariable practice of virtue, and your indefatigable pursuit of knowledge.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter III, to his son, London, December 2, Old Style 1746

text: I call company, walking, riding, etc., employing one's time, and, upon proper occasions, very usefully; but what I cannot forgive in anybody is sauntering, and doing nothing at all, with a thing so precious as time, and so irrecoverable when lost.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter IV, to his son, London, December 9, Old Style 1746

text: There is nothing that people bear more impatiently, or forgive less, than contempt; and an injury is much sooner forgotten than an insult.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter I, to his son, Bath, October 9, Old Style 1746

text: In truth, whatever is worth doing at all, is worth doing well; and nothing can be done well without attention: I therefore carry the necessity of attention down to the lowest things, even to dancing and dress.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter I, to his son, Bath, October 9, Old Style 1746

text: Never maintain an argument with heat and clamor, though you think or know yourself to be in the right: but give your opinion modestly and coolly, which is the only way to convince; and, if that does not do, try to change the conversation, by saying, with good humor, "We shall hardly convince one another, nor is it necessary that we should, so let us talk of something else."
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XVII, to his son, London, October 16, Old Style 1747

text: There is time enough for everything, in the course of the day, if you do but one thing at once; but there is not time enough in the year, if you will do two things at a time.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter IX, to his son, London, April 14, Old Style 1747

text: At the same time that you carefully decline the friendship of knaves and fools, if it can be called friendship, there is no occasion to make either of them your enemies, wantonly and unprovoked; for they are numerous bodies: and I, would rather choose a secure neutrality, than alliance, or war with either of them. You may be a declared enemy to their vices and follies, without being marked out by them as a personal one.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XVI, to his son, London, October 9, Old Style 1747

text: Virtue and learning, like gold, have their intrinsic value but if they are not polished, they certainly lose a great deal of their luster; and even polished brass will pass upon more people than rough gold.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter VI, to his son, London, March 6, Old Style 1747

text: The scholar, without good-breeding, is a pedant; the philosopher, a cynic; the soldier, a brute; and every man disagreeable.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XVI, to his son, London, October 9, Old Style 1747

text: Those who deserve a good character, ought to have the satisfaction of knowing that they have it, both as a reward and as an encouragement.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter VI, to his son, London, March 6, Old Style 1747

text: Remember always, what I have told you a thousand times, that all the talents in the world will want all their lustre, and some part of their use too, if they are not adorned with that easy good-breeding, that engaging manner, and those graces, which seduce and prepossess people in your favor at first sight.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XXIII, to his son, London, December 29, Old Style 1747

text: The friendship which you may contract with people of your own age may be sincere, may be warm; but must be, for some time, reciprocally unprofitable, as there can be no experience on either side.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XX, to his son, London, November 24, Old Style 1747

text: Observe the looks and countenances of those who speak, which is often a surer way of discovering the truth than from what they say.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XVIII, to his son, London, October 30, Old Style 1747

text: You will easily discover every man's prevailing vanity, by observing his favorite topic of conversation; for every man talks most of what he has most a mind to be thought to excel in.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XVII, to his son, London, October 16, Old Style 1747

text: Every man's reason is, and must be, his guide; and I may as well expect that every man should be of my size and complexion, as that he should reason just as I do. Every man seeks for truth; but God only knows who has found it.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XIV, to his son, London, September 21, Old Style 1747

text: Remember, then, as long as you live, that nothing but strict truth can carry you through the world, with either your conscience or your honor unwounded.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XIV, to his son, London, September 21, Old Style 1747

text: Remember, then, that whatever knowledge you do not solidly lay the foundation of before you are eighteen, you will never be the master of while you breathe.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XXI, to his son, London, December 15, Old Style 1747

text: A man is fit for neither business nor pleasure, who either cannot, or does not, command and direct his attention to the present object, and, in some degree, banish for that time all other objects from his thoughts.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter IX, to his son, London, April 14, Old Style 1747

text: Take the tone of the company that you are in, and do not pretend to give it; be serious, gay, or even trifling, as you find the present humor of the company; this is an attention due from every individual to the majority.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XVII, to his son, London, October 16, Old Style 1747

text: If ever we quarrel, do not expect or depend upon any weakness in my nature, for a reconciliation, as children frequently do, and often meet with, from silly parents; I have no such weakness about me: and, as I will never quarrel with you but upon some essential point; if once we quarrel, I will never forgive.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XXII, to his son, London, December 18, Old Style 1747

text: DEAR BOY: Pleasure is the rock which most young people split upon: they launch out with crowded sails in quest of it, but without a compass to direct their course, or reason sufficient to steer the vessel; for want of which, pain and shame, instead of pleasure, are the returns of their voyage.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter VII, to his son, London, March 27, Old Style 1747

text: Civility, which is a disposition to accommodate and oblige others, is essentially the same in every country; but good-breeding, as it is called, which is the manner of exerting that disposition, is different in almost every country, and merely local; and every man of sense imitates and conforms to that local good-breeding of the place which he is at.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XV, to his son, London, October 2, Old Style 1747

text: Do not mistake me, and think that I mean to recommend to you abject and criminal flattery: no; flatter nobody's vices or crimes: on the contrary, abhor and discourage them. But there is no living in the world without a complaisant indulgence for people's weaknesses, and innocent, though ridiculous vanities.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XVII, to his son, London, October 16, Old Style 1747

text: Search, therefore, with the greatest care, into the characters of those whom you converse with; endeavor to discover their predominant passions, their prevailing weaknesses, their vanities, their follies, and their humors, with all the right and wrong, wise and silly springs of human actions, which make such inconsistent and whimsical beings of us rational creatures.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XV, to his son, London, October 2, Old Style 1747

text: True friendship requires certain proportions of age and manners, and can never subsist where they are extremely different, except in the relations of parent and child, where affection on one side, and regard on the other, make up the difference.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XX, to his son, London, November 24, Old Style 1747

text: DEAR BOY: People of your age have, commonly, an unguarded frankness about them; which makes them the easy prey and bubbles of the artful and the experienced; they look upon every knave or fool, who tells them that he is their friend, to be really so; and pay that profession of simulated friendship, with an indiscreet and unbounded confidence, always to their loss, often to their ruin.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XVI, to his son, London, October 9, Old Style 1747

text: If you would particularly gain the affection and friendship of particular people, whether men or women, endeavor to find out the predominant excellency, if they have one, and their prevailing weakness, which everybody has; and do justice to the one, and something more than justice to the other.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XVII, to his son, London, October 16, Old Style 1747

text: What I mean by low company, which should by all means be avoided, is the company of those, who, absolutely insignificant and contemptible in themselves, think they are honored by being in your company; and who flatter every vice and every folly you have, in order to engage you to converse with them.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XVI, to his son, London, October 9, Old Style 1747

text: I would not, at twenty years, be a preaching missionary of abstemiousness and sobriety; and I should let other people do as they would, without formally and sententiously rebuking them for it; but I would be most firmly resolved not to destroy my own faculties and constitution; in complaisance to those who have no regard to their own.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter VII, to his son, London, March 27, Old Style 1747

text: Of all things, banish the egotism out of your conversation, and never think of entertaining people with your own personal concerns, or private, affairs; though they are interesting to you, they are tedious and impertinent to everybody else; besides that, one cannot keep one's own private affairs too secret.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XVII, to his son, London, October 16, Old Style 1747

text: Do not let your vanity and self-love make you suppose that people become your friends at first sight, or even upon a short acquaintance. Real friendship is a slow grower and never thrives unless engrafted upon a stock of known and reciprocal merit.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XVI, to his son, London, October 9, Old Style 1747

text: If a man has a mind to be thought wiser, and a woman handsomer than they really are, their error is a comfortable one to themselves, and an innocent one with regard to other people; and I would rather make them my friends, by indulging them in it, than my enemies, by endeavoring (and that to no purpose) to undeceive them.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XVII, to his son, London, October 16, Old Style 1747

text: Endeavor, as much as you can, to keep company with people above you: there you rise, as much as you sink with people below you; for (as I have mentioned before) you are whatever the company you keep is.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XVI, to his son, London, October 9, Old Style 1747

text: On the other hand, if one of these unmerciful talkers lays hold of you, hear him with patience (and at least seeming attention), if he is worth obliging; for nothing will oblige him more than a patient hearing, as nothing would hurt him more than either to leave him in the midst of his discourse, or to discover your impatience under your affliction.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LIV, to his son, Bath, October 19, Old Style 1748

text: Never hold anybody by the button or the hand, in order to be heard out; for, if people are not willing to hear you, you had much better hold your tongue than them.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LIV, to his son, Bath, October 19, Old Style 1748

text: To go and tell any friend, wife, or mistress, any secret with which they have nothing to do, is discovering to them such an unretentive weakness, as must convince them that you will tell it to twenty others, and consequently that they may reveal it without the risk of being discovered.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter L, to his son, London, September 13, Old Style 1748

text: A prudent reserve is therefore as necessary as a seeming openness is prudent.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LIV, to his son, Bath, October 19, Old Style 1748

text: Many things will happen before you can be fit for business; and when you are fit, whatever my situation may be, it will always be in my power to help you in your first steps; afterward you must help yourself by your own abilities.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XXXIV, to his son, London, March 27, Old Style 1748

text: DEAR Boy: Every excellency, and every virtue, has its kindred vice or weakness; and if carried beyond certain bounds, sinks into one or the other.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XXX, to his son, Bath, February 22, Old Style 1748

text: It is certain, that great numbers of people met together, animate each other, and will do something, either good or bad, but oftener bad; and the respective individuals, who were separately very quiet, when met together in numbers, grow tumultuous as a body, and ripe for any mischief that may be pointed out to them by the leaders; and, if their leaders have no business for them, they will find some for themselves.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter L, to his son, London, September 13, Old Style 1748

text: Every moment that you now lose, is so much character and advantage lost; as, on the other hand, every moment that you now employ usefully, is so much time wisely laid out, at most prodigious interest.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XL, to his son, London, May 27, Old Style 1748

text: The adoption of vice has, I am convinced, ruined ten times more young men than natural inclinations.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LIII, to his son, Bath, October 12, Old Style 1748

text: Sometimes, indeed, extraordinary geniuses have broken out by the force of nature, without the assistance of education; but those instances are too rare for anybody to trust to; and even they would make a much greater figure, if they had the advantage of education into the bargain.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XXXV, to his son, London, April 1, Old Style 1748

text: People are, in general, what they are made, by education and company, from fifteen to five-and-twenty; consider well, therefore, the importance of your next eight or nine years; your whole depends upon them.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XXXV, to his son, London, April 1, Old Style 1748

text: There is hardly any place or any company, where you may not gain knowledge, if you please; almost everybody knows some one thing, and is glad to talk upon that one thing.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XXIX, to his son, Bath, February 18, Old Style 1748

text: Knowledge is like power in this respect, that those who have the most, are most desirous of having more.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XLVII, to his son, London, August 23, Old Style 1748

text: Should you therefore expatiate in the praise of some virtue, which some in company notoriously want; or declaim against any vice, which others are notoriously infected with, your reflections, however general and unapplied, will, by being applicable, be thought personal and leveled at those people.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LV, to his son, Bath, October 29, Old Style 1748

text: As in this case, so in all others, aim always at the highest; get always into the highest company, and address yourself particularly to the highest in it.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LV, to his son, Bath, October 29, Old Style 1748

text: Never yield to that temptation, which to most young men is very strong; of exposing other people's weaknesses and infirmities, for the sake either of diverting the company, or showing your own superiority. You may get the laugh on your side by it for the present; but you will make enemies by it forever; and even those who laugh with you then, will, upon reflection, fear; and consequently hate you; besides that it is ill-natured, and a good heart desires rather to conceal than expose other people's weaknesses or misfortunes.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XLIX, to his son, London, September 5, Old Style 1748

text: The trifling and frivolous mind is always busied, but to little purpose; it takes little objects for great ones, and throws away upon trifles that time and attention which only important things deserve.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XLV, to his son, London, July, 20, Old Style 1748

text: Always look people in the face when you speak to them: the not doing it is thought to imply conscious guilt; besides that you lose the advantage of serving by their countenances what impression your discourse makes upon them. In order to know people's real sentiments, I trust much more to my eyes than to my ears: for they can say whatever they have a mind I should hear; but they can seldom help looking, what they have no intention that I should know.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LIV, to his son, Bath, October 19, Old Style 1748

text: Many a man will confess his crimes to a common friend, but I never knew a man who would tell his silly weaknesses to his most intimate one, as many a friend will tell us our faults without reserve, who will not so much as hint at our follies; that discovery is too mortifying to our self-love, either to tell another, or to be told of one's self.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XLIII, to his son, London, July 1, Old Style 1748

text: Deserve a great deal, and you shall have a great deal; deserve a little, and you shall have but a little; and be good for nothing at all, and, I assure you, you shall have nothing at all.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XLIII, to his son, London, July 1, Old Style 1748

text: Advice is seldom welcome; and those who want it the most always like it the least.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XXVI, to his son, London, January 29, Old Style 1748

text: There are few things that may not be said, in some manner or other; either in a seeming confidence, or a genteel irony, or introduced with wit; and one great part of the knowledge of the world consists in knowing when and where to make use of these different manners.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XLV, to his son, London, July, 20, Old Style 1748

text: A man of the world must, like the chameleon, be able to take every different hue; which is by no means a criminal or abject, but a necessary complaisance; for it relates only to manners and not to morals.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LIV, to his son, Bath, October 19, Old Style 1748

text: A man of sense carefully avoids any particular character in his dress; he is accurately clean for his own sake; but all the rest is for other people's.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXI, to his son, London, December 30, Old Style 1748

text: People always talk best upon what they know most, and it is both pleasing them and improving one's self, to put them upon that subject.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LI, to his son, London, September 20, Old Style 1748

text: In courts, a versatility of genius and softness of manners are absolutely necessary; which some people mistake for abject flattery, and having no opinion of one's own; whereas it is only the decent and genteel manner of maintaining your own opinion, and possibly of bringing other people to it.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XXXVIII, to his son, London, May 10, Old Style 1748

text: Not to seem to perceive the little weaknesses, and the idle but innocent affectations of the company, but even to flatter them, in a certain manner, is not only very allowable, but, in truth, a sort of polite duty.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LV, to his son, Bath, October 29, Old Style 1748

text: A man who will show every knave or fool that he thinks him such, will engage in a most ruinous war, against numbers much superior to those that he and his allies can bring into the field.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LX, to his son, London, December 20, Old Style 1748

text: There is a general tacit trust in conversation, by which a man is obliged not to report anything out of it, though he is not immediately enjoined to secrecy.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LV, to his son, Bath, October 29, Old Style 1748

text: Why may I not feel a very tender and real concern for the misfortune of my friend, and yet at the same time feel a pleasing consciousness at having discharged my duty to him, by comforting and assisting him to the utmost of my power in that misfortune?
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XLIX, to his son, London, September 5, Old Style 1748

text: Be convinced, that there are no persons so insignificant and inconsiderable, but may, some time or other, have it in their power to be of use to you; which they certainly will not, if you have once shown them contempt.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XLIII, to his son, London, July 1, Old Style 1748

text: Never seem wiser, nor more learned, than the people you are with.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XXX, to his son, Bath, February 22, Old Style 1748

text: What I do, and ever shall regret, is the time which, while young, I lost in mere idleness, and in doing nothing.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XXIX, to his son, Bath, February 18, Old Style 1748

text: Good-breeding, and good-nature, do incline us rather to raise and help people up to ourselves, than to mortify and depress them, and, in truth, our own private interest concurs in it, as it is making ourselves so many friends, instead of so many enemies.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XLIII, to his son, London, July 1, Old Style 1748

text: To do whatever you do at all to the utmost perfection, ought to be your aim at this time of your life; if you can reach perfection, so much the better; but at least, by attempting it, you will get much nearer than if you never attempted it at all.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XLIII, to his son, London, July 1, Old Style 1748

text: In your destination particularly, they are in truth half your business: for, if you once gain the affections as well as the esteem of the prince or minister of the court to which you are sent, I will answer for it, that will effectually do the business of the court that sent you; otherwise it is up-hill work.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LVI, to his son, London, November 18, Old Style 1748

text: He who addresses himself singly to another man's reason, without endeavoring to engage his heart in his interest also, is no more likely to succeed, than a man who should apply only to a king's nominal minister, and neglect his favorite.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XLIX, to his son, London, September 5, Old Style 1748

text: Every man is not ambitious, or courteous, or passionate; but every man has pride enough in his composition to feel and resent the least slight and contempt.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XLIX, to his son, London, September 5, Old Style 1748

text: Never be ashamed nor afraid of asking questions: for if they lead to information, and if you accompany them with some excuse, you will never be reckoned an impertinent or rude questioner.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XLV, to his son, London, July, 20, Old Style 1748

text: If you fall into bad and low company there, or anywhere else, you will be irrecoverably lost; whereas, if you keep good company, and company above yourself, your character and your fortune will be immovably fixed.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LVII, to his son, London, November 29, Old Style 1748

text: Vanity, that source of many of our follies, and of some of our crimes, has sunk many a man into company, in every light infinitely, below himself, for the sake of being the first man in it.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LIII, to his son, Bath, October 12, Old Style 1748

text: The height of abilities is to have 'volto sciolto' and 'pensieri stretti'; that is, a frank, open, and ingenuous exterior, with a prudent interior; to be upon your own guard, and yet, by a seeming natural openness, to put people off theirs.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LIV, to his son, Bath, October 19, Old Style 1748

text: The Allied Powers (as we have constantly seen) have, besides the common and declared object of their alliance, some separate and concealed view to which they often sacrifice the general one; which makes them, either directly or indirectly, pull different ways.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XLVIII, to his son, London, August 30, Old Style 1748

text: Men are much more unwilling to have their weaknesses and their imperfections known than their crimes; and if you hint to a man that you think him silly, ignorant, or even ill-bred, or awkward, he will hate you more and longer, than if you tell him plainly, that you think him a rogue.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XLIX, to his son, London, September 5, Old Style 1748

text: Depend upon it, you will sink or rise to the level of the company which you commonly keep: people will judge of you, and not unreasonably, by that.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LIII, to his son, Bath, October 12, Old Style 1748

text: Some complaisance and attention to fools is prudent, and not mean; as a silent abhorrence of individual knaves is often necessary and not criminal.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LX, to his son, London, December 20, Old Style 1748

text: Observe any meetings of people, and you will always find their eagerness and impetuosity rise or fall in proportion to their numbers: when the numbers are very great, all sense and reason seem to subside, and one sudden frenzy to seize on all, even the coolest of them.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter L, to his son, London, September 13, Old Style 1748

text: Such is my desire, my anxiety for your perfection, that I never think I have said enough, though you may possibly think that I have said too much; and though, in truth, if your own good sense is not sufficient to direct you, in many of these plain points, all that I or anybody else can say will be insufficient.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LVI, to his son, London, November 18, Old Style 1748

text: Take care never to seem dark and mysterious; which is not only a very unamiable character, but a very suspicious one too; if you seem mysterious with others, they will be really so with you, and you will know nothing.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LIV, to his son, Bath, October 19, Old Style 1748

text: In order to judge of the inside of others, study your own; for men in general are very much alike; and though one has one prevailing passion, and another has another, yet their operations are much the same; and whatever engages or disgusts, pleases or offends you, in others will, 'mutatis mutandis', engage, disgust, please, or offend others, in you.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXI, to his son, London, May 22, Old Style 1749

text: I aver that no man is, in any degree, fit for either business or conversation, who cannot and does not direct and command his attention to the present object, be that what it will.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXXII, to his son, London, September 22, Old Style 1749

text: I should desire nothing better, in any negotiation, than to have to do with one of those men of warm, quick passions; which I would take care to set in motion.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXI, to his son, London, May 22, Old Style 1749

text: DEAR BOY: Those who suppose that men in general act rationally, because they are called rational creatures, know very little of the world, and if they act themselves upon that supposition, will nine times in ten find themselves grossly mistaken.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XCIII, to his son, London, December 5, Old Style 1749

text: Trust those only to some tried friend, more experienced than yourself, and who, being in a different walk of life from you, is not likely to become your rival; for I would not advise you to depend so much upon the heroic virtue of mankind, as to hope or believe that your competitor will ever be your friend, as to the object of that competition.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XCVII, to his son, London, December 19, Old Style 1749

text: Some people are to be reasoned, some flattered, some intimidated, and some teased into a thing; but, in general, all are to be brought into it at last, if skillfully applied to, properly managed, and indefatigably attacked in their several weak places.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXI, to his son, London, May 22, Old Style 1749

text: Business and pleasure, rightly understood, mutually assist each other, instead of being enemies, as silly or dull people often think them. No man tastes pleasures truly, who does not earn them by previous business, and few people do business well, who do nothing else.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXVII, to his son, London, August 7, Old Style 1749

text: The principal of these things is the mastery of one's temper, and that coolness of mind, and serenity of countenance, which hinders us from discovering by words, actions, or even looks, those passions or sentiments by which we are inwardly moved or agitated; and the discovery of which gives cooler and abler people such infinite advantages over us, not only in great business, but in all the most common occurrences of life.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXI, to his son, London, May 22, Old Style 1749

text: Moral virtues are the foundation of society in general, and of friendship in particular; but attentions, manners, and graces, both adorn and strengthen them.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXV, to his son, London, July 20, Old Style 1749

text: If a man accosts you, and talks to you ever so dully or frivolously, it is worse than rudeness, it is brutality, to show him, by a manifest inattention to what he says, that you think him a fool or a blockhead, and not worth hearing.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXXVIII, to his son, London, November 3, Old Style 1749

text: It is the character of an able man to despise little things in great business: but then he knows what things are little, and what not.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XCII, to his son, London, November 27, Old Style 1749

text: Consult your reason betimes: I do not say that it will always prove an unerring guide; for human reason is not infallible; but it will prove the least erring guide that you can follow.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXIV, to his son, London, February 7, Old Style 1749

text: I will advise you seriously, as a friend of some experience, and I will converse with you cheerfully as a companion; the authority of a parent shall forever be laid aside; for, wherever it is exerted, it is useless; since, if you have neither sense nor sentiments enough to follow my advice as a friend, your unwilling obedience to my orders as a father will be a very awkward and unavailing one both to yourself and me.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXXVII, to his son, London, October 24, Old Style 1749

text: Be upon your guard against those who upon very slight acquaintance, obtrude their unasked and unmerited friendship and confidence upon you; for they probably cram you with them only for their own eating; but, at the same time, do not roughly reject them upon that general supposition.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XCVII, to his son, London, December 19, Old Style 1749

text: Whoever is admitted or sought for, in company, upon any other account than that of his merit and manners, is never respected there, but only made use of.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXVIII, to his son, London, August 20, Old Style 1749

text: Pry into the recesses of their hearts yourself, as far as you are able, and never implicitly adopt a character upon common fame; which, though generally right as to the great outlines of characters, is always wrong in some particulars.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XCVII, to his son, London, December 19, Old Style 1749

text: The art of pleasing is more particularly necessary in your intended profession than perhaps in any other; it is, in truth, the first half of your business; for if you do not please the court you are sent to, you will be of very little use to the court you are sent from.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXX, to his son, London, May 15, Old Style 1749

text: A man of parts and efficiency need not flatter everybody at court; but he must take great care to offend nobody personally; it being in the power of every man to hurt him, who cannot serve him.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXIX, to his son, London, August 21, Old Style 1749

text: People will not be called out to your service, only when you want them; and, if you expect to receive strength from them, they must receive either pleasure or advantage from you.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXXIX, to his son, London, November 14, Old Style 1749

text: A young man should never be wanting in those attentions; they cost little and bring in a great deal, by getting you people's good word and affection.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXIX, to his son, London, April 27, Old Style 1749

text: A man's general character may be that of the honestest man of the world: do not dispute it; you might be thought envious or ill-natured; but, at the same time, do not take this probity upon trust to such a degree as to put your life, fortune, or reputation in his power. This honest man may happen to be your rival in power, in interest, or in love; three passions that often put honesty to most severe trials, in which it is too often cast; but first analyze this honest man yourself; and then only you will be able to judge how far you may, or may not, with safety trust him.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XCVII, to his son, London, December 19, Old Style 1749

text: This is so true, that you may think you connect yourself with two friends to-day, and be obliged tomorrow to make your option between them as enemies; observe, therefore, such a degree of reserve with your friends as not to put yourself in their power, if they should become your enemies; and such a degree of moderation with your enemies, as not to make it impossible for them to become your friends.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXIX, to his son, London, August 21, Old Style 1749

text: Whereas now, without any extraordinary effort of genius, I have discovered that nature was the same three thousand years ago as it is at present; that men were but men then as well as now; that modes and customs vary often, but that human nature is always the same.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXIV, to his son, London, February 7, Old Style 1749

text: Whereas dissimulation is a shield, as secrecy is armor; and it is no more possible to preserve secrecy in business, without same degree of dissimulation, than it is to succeed in business without secrecy.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXI, to his son, London, May 22, Old Style 1749

text: Some men are more captious than others; some are always wrongheaded; but every man living has such a share of vanity, as to be hurt by marks of slight and contempt.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XCVII, to his son, London, December 19, Old Style 1749

text: The time should likewise be judiciously chosen; every man has his 'mollia tempora', but that is far from being all day long; and you would choose your time very ill, if you applied to a man about one business, when his head was full of another, or when his heart was full of grief, anger, or any other disagreeable sentiment.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXI, to his son, London, May 22, Old Style 1749

text: This dignity of manners, which I recommend so much to you, is not only as different from pride, as true courage is from blustering, or true wit from joking; but is absolutely inconsistent with it; for nothing vilifies and degrades more than pride.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXVIII, to his son, London, August 20, Old Style 1749

text: You must never usurp to yourself those conveniences and 'agremens' which are of common right; such as the best places, the best dishes, etc., but on the contrary, always decline them yourself, and offer them to others; who, in their turns, will offer them to you; so that, upon the whole, you will in your turn enjoy your share of the common right.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXXVIII, to his son, London, November 3, Old Style 1749

text: Indiscriminate familiarity either offends your superiors, or else dubbs you their dependent and led captain. It gives your inferiors just, but troublesome and improper claims of equality.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXVIII, to his son, London, August 20, Old Style 1749

text: A friend of yours and mine has very justly defined good-breeding to be, THE RESULT OF MUCH GOOD SENSE, SOME GOOD NATURE, AND A LITTLE SELF-DENIAL FOR THE SAKE OF OTHERS, AND WITH A VIEW TO OBTAIN THE SAME INDULGENCE FROM THEM.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXXVIII, to his son, London, November 3, Old Style 1749

text: As for politeness: whoever keeps good company, and is not polite, must have formed a resolution, and take some pains not to be so; otherwise he would naturally and insensibly take the air, the address, and the turn of those he converses with.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XCIX, to his son, London, December 26, Old Style 1749

text: DEAR BOY: A vulgar, ordinary way of thinking, acting, or speaking, implies a low education, and a habit of low company.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXXIII, to his son, London, September 27, Old Style 1749

text: The man who cannot join business and pleasure is either a formal coxcomb in the one, or a sensual beast in the other.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXIX, to his son, London, April 27, Old Style 1749

text: No man is distrait with the man he fears, or the woman he loves; which is a proof that every man can get the better of that DISTRACTION, when he thinks it worth his while to do so; and, take my word for it, it is always worth his while.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXXII, to his son, London, September 22, Old Style 1749

text: We must not suppose that, because a man is a rational animal, he will therefore always act rationally; or, because he has such or such a predominant passion, that he will act invariably and consequentially in the pursuit of it.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XCVII, to his son, London, December 19, Old Style 1749

text: Those necessary connections can never be formed, or preserved, but by an uninterrupted series of complaisance, attentions, politeness, and some constraint. You must engage their hearts, if you would have their support.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXXIX, to his son, London, November 14, Old Style 1749

text: Mutual complaisances, attentions, and sacrifices of little conveniences, are as natural an implied compact between civilized people, as protection and obedience are between kings and subjects; whoever, in either case, violates that compact, justly forfeits all advantages arising from it.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXXVIII, to his son, London, November 3, Old Style 1749

text: If ever a man and his wife, or a man and his mistress, who pass nights as well as days together, absolutely lay aside all good-breeding, their intimacy will soon degenerate into a coarse familiarity, infallibly productive of contempt or disgust.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXXVIII, to his son, London, November 3, Old Style 1749

text: For my own part, I would rather be in company with a dead man, than with an absent one; for if the dead man gives me no pleasure; at least he shows me no contempt; whereas, the absent man, silently indeed, but very plainly, tells me that he does not think me worth his attention.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXXII, to his son, London, September 22, Old Style 1749

text: Care and reflection, if properly used, will get the better: and a man may as surely get a habit of letting his reason prevail over his constitution, as of letting, as most people do, the latter prevail over the former.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXI, to his son, London, May 22, Old Style 1749

text: Suspect, in general, those who remarkably affect any one virtue; who raise it above all others, and who, in a manner, intimate that they possess it exclusively. I say suspect them, for they are commonly impostors; but do not be sure that they are always so; for I have sometimes known saints really religious, blusterers really brave, reformers of manners really honest, and prudes really chaste.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XCVII, to his son, London, December 19, Old Style 1749

text: If you find yourself subject to sudden starts of passion or madness (for I see no difference between them but in their duration), resolve within yourself, at least, never to speak one word while you feel that emotion within you.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXI, to his son, London, May 22, Old Style 1749

text: It is a decided folly to lose a friend for a jest; but, in my mind, it is not a much less degree of folly to make an enemy of an indifferent and neutral person, for the sake of a 'bon mot'.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXI, to his son, London, May 22, Old Style 1749

text: A man of sense soon discovers, because he carefully observes, where, and how long, he is welcome; and takes care to leave the company, at least as soon as he is wished out of it. Fools never perceive where they are either ill-timed or illplaced.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXV, to his son, London, July 20, Old Style 1749

text: Seek first, then, for the predominant passion of the character which you mean to engage and influence, and address yourself to it; but without defying or despising the inferior passions; get them in your interest too, for now and then they will have their turns.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XCVII, to his son, London, December 19, Old Style 1749

text: If people had no vices but their own, few would have so many as they have. For my own part, I would sooner wear other people's clothes than their vices; and they would sit upon me just as well.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXX, to his son, London, May 15, Old Style 1749

text: A fool squanders away, without credit or advantage to himself, more than a man of sense spends with both. The latter employs his money as he does his time, and never spends a shilling of the one, nor a minute of the other, but in something that is either useful or rationally pleasing to himself or others.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXII, to his son, London, January 10, Old Style 1749

text: You are now laying the foundation of your future character and fortune; and one single stone wanting in that foundation is of more consequence than fifty in the superstructure; which can always be mended and embellished if the foundation is solid.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter LXXVI, to his son, London, July 30, Old Style 1749

text: Conscious virtue is the only solid foundation of all happiness; for riches, power, rank, or whatever, in the common acceptation of the word, is supposed to constitute happiness, will never quiet, much less cure, the inward pangs of guilt.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter XCIX, to his son, London, December 26, Old Style 1749

text: Without this purity, you can have no dignity of character; and without dignity of character it is impossible to rise in the world.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter C, to his son, London, January 8, Old Style 1750

text: In business (talents supposed) nothing is more effectual or successful, than a good, though concealed opinion of one's self, a firm resolution, and an unwearied perseverance.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXV, to his son, London, June 5, Old Style 1750

text: To succeed, a man, especially a young one, should have inward firmness, steadiness, and intrepidity, with exterior modesty and SEEMING diffidence.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXIV, to his son, London, May 24., Old Style 1750

text: There is a certain dignity to be kept up in pleasures, as well as in business.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CIV, to his son, London, February 5, Old Style 1750

text: Pleasure is necessarily reciprocal; no one feels, who does not at the same time give it.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXVII, to his son, London, July 9, Old Style 1750

text: In purity of character and in politeness of manners labor to excel all, if you wish to equal many.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter C, to his son, London, January 8, Old Style 1750

text: Whatever real merit you have, other people will discover, and people always magnify their own discoveries, as they lessen those of others.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXIII, to his son, London, May 17, Old Style 1750

text: The manner is often as important as the matter, sometimes more so; a favor may make an enemy, and an injury may make a friend, according to the different manner in which they are severally done.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield

text: DEAR BOY: Great talents and great virtues (if you should have them) will procure you the respect and the admiration of mankind; but it is the lesser talents, the 'leniores virtutes', which must procure you their love and affection.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield

text: Your knowledge will have but very little influence upon the mind, if your manners prejudice the heart against you; but, on the other hand, how easily will you DUPE the understanding, where you have first engaged the heart? and hearts are by no means to be gained by that mere common civility which everybody practices.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield

text: The most general rule that I can give you for the world, and which your experience will convince you of the truth of, is, Never to give the tone to the company, but to take it from them; and to labor more to put them in conceit with themselves, than to make them admire you.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXVII, to his son, London, July 9, Old Style 1750

text: Every man becomes, to a certain degree, what the people he generally converses with are.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXIV, to his son, London, May 24., Old Style 1750

text: Whereas, concealing the truth, upon proper occasions, is as prudent and as innocent, as telling a lie, upon any occasion, is infamous and foolish.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter C, to his son, London, January 8, Old Style 1750

text: Serious reflection will always give courage in a good cause; and the courage arising from reflection is of a much superior nature to the animal and constitutional courage of a foot soldier.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield

text: Do you, on the contrary, never talk of business but to those with whom you are to transact it; and learn to seem vacuus and idle, when you have the most business.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield

text: Lose no time, my dear child, I conjure you, in forming your taste, your manners, your mind, your everything; you have but two years' time to do it in; for whatever you are, to a certain degree, at twenty, you will be, more or less, all the rest of your life.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CV, to his son, London, February 8, Old Style 1750

text: There is nothing so delicate as your moral character, and nothing which it is your interest so much to preserve pure. Should you be suspected of injustice, malignity, perfidy, lying, etc., all the parts and knowledge in the world will never procure you esteem, friendship, or respect.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter C, to his son, London, January 8, Old Style 1750

text: The knowledge of a scholar, the courage of a hero, and the virtue of a Stoic, will be admired; but if the knowledge be accompanied with arrogance, the courage with ferocity, and the virtue with inflexible severity, the man will never be loved.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield

text: If two men of equal talents negotiate together, he who best understands the language in which the negotiation is carried on, will infallibly get the better of the other.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXII, to his son, London, May 8, Old Style 1750

text: Honor must be the principle of such connections; and there must be a mutual dependence, that present and separate interest shall not be able to break them. There must be a joint system of action; and, in case of different opinions, each must recede a little, in order at last to form an unanimous one.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXIX, to his son, London, October 22, Old Style 1750

text: MY DEAR FRIEND: Very few people are good economists of their fortune, and still fewer of their time; and yet of the two, the latter is the most precious.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CIV, to his son, London, February 5, Old Style 1750

text: The affectation of courage will make even a brave man pass only for a bully; as the affectation of wit will make a man of parts pass for a coxcomb.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXIII, to his son, London, May 17, Old Style 1750

text: On the other hand, let no complaisance, no gentleness of temper, no weak desire of pleasing on your part, no wheedling, coaxing, nor flattery, on other people's, make you recede one jot from any point that reason and prudence have bid you pursue; but return to the charge, persist, persevere, and you will find most things attainable that are possible. A yielding, timid meekness is always abused and insulted by the unjust and the unfeeling; but when sustained by the 'fortiter in re', is always respected, commonly successful.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield

text: Bowing again to those who bow to you, answering dryly those who speak to you, and saying nothing offensive to anybody, is such negative good-breeding that it is only not being a brute; as it would be but a very poor commendation of any man's cleanliness to say that he did not stink.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield

text: A man who does not solidly establish, and really deserve, a character of truth, probity, good manners, and good morals, at his first setting out in the world, may impose, and shine like a meteor for a very short time, but will very soon vanish, and be extinguished with contempt.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXIII, to his son, London, May 17, Old Style 1750

text: People hate those who make them feel their own inferiority.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXI, to his son, London, April 30, Old Style 1750

text: Be extremely upon your guard against vanity, the common failing of inexperienced youth; but particularly against that kind of vanity that dubs a man a coxcomb; a character which, once acquired, is more indelible than that of the priesthood.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXIII, to his son, London, May 17, Old Style 1750

text: From the moment that you are dressed and go out, pocket all your knowledge with your watch, and never pull it out in company unless desired: the producing of the one unasked, implies that you are weary of the company; and the producing of the other unrequired, will make the company weary of you.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXX, to his son, London, November 1, Old Style 1750

text: Some people cannot gain upon themselves to be easy and civil to those who are either their rivals, competitors, or opposers, though, independently of those accidental circumstances, they would like and esteem them. They betray a shyness and an awkwardness in company with them, and catch at any little thing to expose them; and so, from temporary and only occasional opponents, make them their personal enemies.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield

text: Consider your own situation in every particular, and judge whether it is not essentially your interest, by your own good-breeding to others, to secure theirs to you and that, let me assure you, is the only way of doing it; for people will repay, and with interest too, inattention with inattention, neglect with neglect, and ill manners with worse: which may engage you in very disagreeable affairs.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield

text: In all courts you must expect to meet with connections without friendship, enmities without hatred, honor without virtue, appearances saved, and realities sacrificed; good manners with bad morals; and all vice and virtues so disguised, that whoever has only reasoned upon both would know neither when he first met them at court.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXVI, to his son, London, June 11, Old Style 1750

text: Dispatch is the soul of business; and nothing contributes more to dispatch than method.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CIV, to his son, London, February 5, Old Style 1750

text: A tradesman who would succeed in his way, must begin by establishing a character of integrity and good manners; without the former, nobody will go to his shop at all; without the latter, nobody will go there twice.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXIII, to his son, London, May 17, Old Style 1750

text: From what has been said, I conclude with this observation, that gentleness of manners, with firmness of mind, is a short, but full description of human perfection on this side of religious and moral duties.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield

text: Take great care never to tell in one company what you see or hear in another, much less to divert the present company at the expense of the last; but let discretion and secrecy be known parts of your character.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXI, to his son, London, April 30, Old Style 1750

text: People insensibly contract, not only the air, the manners, and the vices, of those with whom they commonly converse, but their virtues too, and even their way of thinking.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CII, to his son, London, January 18, Old Style 1750

text: Nothing will escape me: I shall pry for your defects, in order to correct them, as curiously as I shall seek for your perfections, in order to applaud and reward them, with this difference only, that I shall publicly mention the latter, and never hint at the former, but in a letter to, or a tete-d-tete with you. I will never put you out of countenance before company; and I hope you will never give me reason to be out of countenance for you, as any one of the above-mentioned defects would make me.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXXIII, to his son, London, November 12, Old Style 1750

text: I have known many people patronized, pushed up, and preferred by those who could have given no other reason for it, than that they were used to them.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield

text: Whenever you meet with a man eminent in any way, feed him, and feed upon him at the same time; it will not only improve you, but give you a reputation of knowledge, and of loving it in others.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CVII, to his son, London, March 8, Old Style 1750

text: Whereas, in truth, all that they get is ridicule and contempt, not without a good degree of distrust; for one must naturally conclude, that he who will tell any lie from idle vanity, will not scruple telling a greater for interest.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter C, to his son, London, January 8, Old Style 1750

text: On the other hand, the cunning, crafty man thinks to gain all his ends by the 'suaviter in modo' only; HE BECOMES ALL THINGS TO ALL MEN; he seems to have no opinion of his own, and servilely adopts the present opinion of the present person; he insinuates himself only into the esteem of fools, but is soon detected, and surely despised by everybody else.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield

text: I could wish that you would say, to the five or six men or women with whom you are the most acquainted, that you are sensible that, from youth and inexperience, you must make many mistakes in good-breeding; that you beg of them to correct you, without reserve, wherever they see you fail; and that you shall take such admonition as the strongest proofs of their friendship.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CI, to his son, London, January 11, Old Style 1750

text: Those who, in the common course of the world, will call themselves your friends; or whom, according to the common notions of friendship, you may possibly think such, will never tell you of your faults, still less of your weaknesses. But, on the contrary, more desirous to make you their friend, than to prove themselves yours, they will flatter both, and, in truth, not be sorry for either.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXVII, to his son, London, July 9, Old Style 1750

text: The weaker party must be taken by the heart, his head giving no hold; and he must be governed by being made to believe that he governs.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXIX, to his son, London, October 22, Old Style 1750

text: If, in negotiations, you are looked upon as a liar and a trickster, no confidence will be placed in you, nothing will be communicated to you, and you will be in the situation of a man who has been burned in the cheek; and who, from that mark, cannot afterward get an honest livelihood if he would, but must continue a thief.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter C, to his son, London, January 8, Old Style 1750

text: You will find that he takes care never to say or do any thing that can be construed into a slight, or a negligence; or that can, in any degree, mortify people's vanity and self-love; on the contrary, you will perceive that he makes people pleased with him, by making them first pleased with themselves: he shows respect, regard, esteem and attention, where they are severally proper: he sows them with care, and he reaps them in plenty.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CII, to his son, London, January 18, Old Style 1750

text: A cool, steady resolution should show that where you have a right to command you will be obeyed; but at the same time, a gentleness in the manner of enforcing that obedience should make it a cheerful one, and soften as much as possible the mortifying consciousness of inferiority.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield

text: People easily pardon, in young men, the common irregularities of the senses: but they do not forgive the least vice of the heart. The heart never grows better by age; I fear rather worse; always harder.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXIII, to his son, London, May 17, Old Style 1750

text: Inquire into the characters of the several Academicians, before you form a connection with any of them; and be most upon your guard against those who make the most court to you.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield

text: Real merit of any kind, 'ubi est non potest diu celari'; it will be discovered, and nothing can depreciate it but a man's exhibiting it himself. It may not always be rewarded as it ought, but it will always be known.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXI, to his son, London, April 30, Old Style 1750

text: It is knowledge, more than quick, flashy parts, that makes a man of business. A man who is master of his matter, twill, with inferior parts, be too hard in parliament, and indeed anywhere else, for a man of-better parts, who knows his subject but superficially: and if to his knowledge he joins eloquence and elocution, he must necessarily soon be at the head of that assembly; but without those two, no knowledge is sufficient.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXXVIII, to his son, London, January 21, Old Style. 1751

text: A man of sense takes the time necessary for doing the thing he is about, well; and his haste to dispatch a business only appears by the continuity of his application to it: he pursues it with a cool steadiness, and finishes it before he begins any other.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXXIX, to his son, London, August 28, Old Style 1751

text: Second-rate knowledge and middling talents carry a man further at courts, and in the busy part of the world, than superior knowledge and shining parts.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXLVIII, to his son, Greenwich, June 20, Old Style 1751

text: A man who is really diffident, timid, and bashful, be his merit what it will, never can push himself in the world; his despondency throws him into inaction; and the forward, the bustling, and the petulant, will always get the better of him.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXXX, to his son, London, February 4, Old Style 1751

text: In short, take care to make as many personal friends, and as few personal enemies, as possible. I do not mean, by personal friends, intimate and confidential friends, of which no man can hope to have half a dozen in the whole course of his life; but I mean friends, in the common acceptation of the word; that is, people who speak well of you, and who would rather do you good than harm, consistently with their own interest, and no further.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXXIX, to his son, London, August 28, Old Style 1751

text: Let your connections be with people above you; by that means you will acquire a habit of respect and politeness. With one's equals, one is apt to become negligent, and the mind grows torpid.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
speaker: Madame Lambert, quoted by Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXLV, to his son, Greenwich, June 6, Old Style 1751

text: Masters are like mistresses: whatever services they may be indebted to you for, they cease to love when you cease to be agreeable.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXLV, to his son, Greenwich, June 6, Old Style 1751

text: In premeditated, or in formal business, people conceal, or at least endeavor to conceal, their characters: whereas pleasures discover them, and the heart breaks out through the guard of the understanding.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXXXVI, to his son, London, March 25, Old Style 1751

text: A man who displays his own merit is a coxcomb, and a man who does not know it is a fool. A man of sense knows it, exerts it, avails himself of it, but never boasts of it; and always SEEMS rather to under than over value it, though in truth, he sets the right value upon it.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXXX, to his son, London, February 4, Old Style 1751

text: A man of sense may be in haste, but can never be in a hurry, because he knows that whatever he does in a hurry, he must necessarily do very ill.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXXIX, to his son, London, August 28, Old Style 1751

text: I do not mean by this to recommend to you 'le fade doucereux', the insipid softness of a gentle fool; no, assert your own opinion, oppose other people's when wrong; but let your manner, your air, your terms, and your tone of voice, be soft and gentle, and that easily and naturally, not affectedly.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXLI, to his son, London, May 6, Old Style 1751

text: Remember to bring your mother some little presents; they need not be of value, but only marks of your affection and duty for one who has always been tenderly fond of you.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CLI, to his son, Greenwich, July 8, Old Style 1751

text: People in general take characters, as they do most things, upon trust, rather than be at the trouble of examining them themselves; and the decisions of four or five fashionable people, in every place, are final, more particularly with regard to characters, which all can hear, and but few judge of.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CXXVII, to his son, London, January 14, Old Style 1751

text: Two, the most intimate friends in the world, can freely tell each other their faults, and even their crimes, but cannot possibly tell each other of certain little weaknesses; awkwardnesses, and blindnesses of self-love; to authorize that unreserved freedom, the relation between us is absolutely necessary.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CLII, to his son, Greenwich, July 15, Old Style 1751

text: Whatever business you have, do it the first moment you can; never by halves, but finish it without interruption, if possible.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CLXII, to his son, London, March 5, Old Style 1752

text: Such pertinent questions are far from being illbred or troublesome to those of whom you ask them; on the contrary, they are a tacit compliment to their knowledge; and people have a better opinion of a young man, when they see him desirous to be informed.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CLV, to his son, London, January 2, Old Style 1752

text: Few, (especially young) people know how to love, or how to hate; their love is an unbounded weakness, fatal to the person they love; their hate is a hot, rash, and imprudent violence, always fatal to themselves.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CLXXIX, to his son, London, September 29, 1752

text: Company is, in truth, a constant state of negotiation; and, if you attend to it in that view, will qualify you for any. By the same means that you make a friend, guard against an enemy, or gain a mistress; you will make an advantageous treaty, baffle those who counteract you, and gain the court you are sent to.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CLXXVIII, to his son, London, September 26, 1752

text: It is the same in business; where he who can command his temper and his countenance the best, will always have an infinite advantage over the other.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CLXXIX, to his son, London, September 29, 1752

text: A man requires very little knowledge and experience of the world, to understand glaring, high-colored, and decided characters; they are but few, and they strike at first: but to distinguish the almost imperceptible shades, and the nice gradations of virtue and vice, sense and folly, strength and weakness (of which characters are commonly composed), demands some experience, great observation, and minute attention.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CLXIII, to his son, London, March 16, Old Style 1752

text: Inattention is always looked upon, though sometimes unjustly, as the effect of pride and contempt; and where it is thought so, is never forgiven.
author: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
locator: Letter CLXXXI, to his son, Bath, November 11, Old Style 1752

text: Another thing, which I most earnestly recommend to you, not only in Germany, but in every part of the world where you may ever be, is not only real, but seeming attention, to whoever you speak to, or to whoever speaks to you.
